results.prompt: Use the correct Slurm accounting command for: Show whether user dave is listed in the research account
results.agent_response:
Use sacctmgr (accounting manager). Two equivalent read-only ways:

- List users associated with account "research":
  sacctmgr show association account=research format=User,Account,Cluster

- Or show dave's associations:
  sacctmgr show user name=dave withassoc format=User,Account

If the output contains "dave" under the research Account, then user dave is listed in the research account.

### Shared File System[#shared](https://slurm.schedmd.com/hdf5_profile_user_guide.html)
The HDF5 Profile Plugin requires a common shared file system on all
the compute nodes. While a job is running, the plugin writes a
file into this file system for each step of the job on each node. When
the job ends, the merge process is launched and the node-step files
are combined into one HDF5 file for the job.
The root of the directory structure is declared in the ProfileHDF5Dir
option in the acct_gather.conf file. The directory will be created by
Slurm if it doesn't exist. Each user will have
their own directory created in the ProfileHDF5Dir which contains
the HDF5 files. All the directories and files are created by the
SlurmdUser which is usually root. The user specific directories, as well
as the files inside, are chowned to the user running the job so they
can access the files. Since user root is usually creating these

## QOS examples[#examples](https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html)
QOS manipulation examples. All QOS operations are done using
the sacctmgr command. The default output of 'sacctmgr show qos' is
very long given the large number of limits and options available
so it is best to use the format option which filters the display.
By default when a cluster is added to the database a default
qos named normal is created.
```text
$ sacctmgr show qos format=name,priority Name Priority ---------- ---------- normal 0
```
Add a new QOS
```text
$ sacctmgr add qos zebra Adding QOS(s) zebra Settings Description = QOS Name $ sacctmgr show qos format=name,priority Name Priority ---------- ---------- normal 0 zebra 0
```
Set QOS priority
```text
$ sacctmgr modify qos zebra set priority=10 Modified qos... zebra $ sacctmgr show qos format=name,priority Name Priority ---------- ---------- normal 0 zebra 10
```

the compute nodes. While a job is running, the plugin writes a
file into this file system for each step of the job on each node. When

## Coordinator[#coord](https://slurm.schedmd.com/user_permissions.html)
A special privileged user, usually an account manager, that can add
users or sub-accounts to the account they are coordinator over.
This should be a trusted person since they can change limits on account and
user associations, as well as cancel, requeue or reassign accounts of jobs
inside their realm. Note that a coordinator may not increase job limits above
the parent ones.
Set using a table in Slurm's database defining users and accounts for
which they can serve as coordinators.
For configuration information, see the
[sacctmgr](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sacctmgr.html) man page.

## Infrastructure [#infrastructure](https://slurm.schedmd.com/accounting.html)
With the SlurmDBD, we are able to collect data from multiple
clusters in a single location.
This does impose some constraints on the user naming and IDs.
Accounting is maintained by user name (not user ID), but a
given user name should refer to the same person across all
of the computers.
Authentication relies upon user ID numbers, so those must
be uniform across all computers communicating with each
SlurmDBD, at least for users requiring authentication.
In particular, the configured SlurmUser must have the
same name and ID across all clusters.
If you plan to have administrators of user accounts, limits,
etc. they must also have consistent names and IDs across all
clusters.
If you plan to restrict access to accounting records (e.g.
only permit a user to view records of his jobs), then all
users should have consistent names and IDs.

results.agent_response:
Here’s a concise guide to submitting batch jobs with sbatch and common options/examples.

1) Write a batch script
- Start with a shebang and #SBATCH directives (one per line) before any non-comment content:
  #!/bin/bash
  #SBATCH -J myjob                # job name
  #SBATCH -p normal               # partition
  #SBATCH -t 02:00:00             # walltime (HH:MM:SS)
  #SBATCH -N 1                    # nodes
  #SBATCH --ntasks=1              # tasks (MPI ranks)
  #SBATCH --cpus-per-task=4      # threads per task
  #SBATCH --mem=16G               # memory
  #SBATCH -o myjob.%j.out         # stdout ( %j -> jobid )
  #SBATCH -e myjob.%j.err         # stderr
  #SBATCH --mail-type=END,FAIL    # email on end/fail
  #SBATCH -A myaccount            # account (if required)

- After directives, do work commands. Use srun for parallel/mpi steps:
  module load python
  srun python train.py --epochs 10

Notes:
- #SBATCH lines must appear before the first non-comment, non-whitespace line.
- Command-line sbatch options override #SBATCH directives in the script.

2) Submit the job
- Submit file:
  sbatch myjob.sh
- Typical reply (example): "Submitted batch job 12345" — the returned number is your job ID.

3) Submit examples / variants
- GPU job (request 1 GPU):
  # SBATCH --gres=gpu:1
- Quick single command (no script file):
  echo -e "#!/bin/bash\nsleep 60" | sbatch
- Pass args to script:
  sbatch myscript.sh arg1 arg2
  (inside script $1, $2 are available)
- Array job:
  #SBATCH --array=1-100%10
  use $SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID inside the script.

4) Check status and logs
- squeue -u $USER             (show your queued/running jobs)
- squeue -j <jobid>           (specific job)
- sacct -j <jobid>            (historical/accounting info after job completes)
- Output/error files are written as you specified with -o/-e.

5) Quick tips / common formats
- Time: HH:MM:SS or D-HH:MM:SS (or minutes)
- Memory: M, G, T suffixes (e.g., 16000M or 16G)
- GPUs: --gres=gpu:<count> (or gpu:V100:1 on some clusters)
- Use module load or environment setup in the script.
- If your cluster requires an account/partition or specific QOS, include -A / -p / --qos.
- For parallel work, use srun inside the script rather than running mpiexec directly.

If you want, tell me:
- the kind of job (CPU, GPU, MPI, array), resources you need (CPUs, memory, time, GPUs), and I can generate a ready-to-submit sbatch script for you.

results.prompt: Slurm tutorial
results.agent_response:
Good — here’s a compact, practical Slurm tutorial you can use as a quick reference. If you want an expanded guide (GPU examples, MPI, arrays, debugging checklist) tell me which area and I’ll dive deeper.

1) Key concepts
- Controller (slurmctld) schedules jobs; compute nodes run them.
- Partition = scheduling queue (e.g., cpu, gpu, debug).
- Job = a submitted workload; can have steps. Jobs have IDs, states (PENDING, RUNNING, COMPLETED, FAILED, CANCELLED).
- Resources: CPUs, memory, time, GPUs, TRES, QOS, accounts.
- Batch jobs vs interactive allocations:
  - sbatch: submit a batch script (noninteractive).
  - srun: run a command in an allocation / launch parallel tasks.
  - salloc: get an interactive allocation (then srun or shell inside it).

2) Basic commands
- Submit: sbatch myscript.sh
- Interactive allocation: salloc -N1 -n4 --time=01:00:00
- Immediate run in allocation: srun --ntasks=4 ./myprog
- Show queue: squeue (filter: -u alice, -p gpu)
- Show partitions/nodes: sinfo
- Cancel job: scancel <jobid>
- Show detailed job info: scontrol show job <jobid>
- Accounting/history: sacct -j <jobid> or sacct -u alice --starttime=2024-01-01
- Scheduler diagnostics: sdiag, sprio, sshare
- Licenses/reservations: scontrol show reservation / scontrol show license

3) Minimal sbatch script example
#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --job-name=test-job
#SBATCH --output=job-%j.out
#SBATCH --error=job-%j.err
#SBATCH --nodes=1
#SBATCH --ntasks=1
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=4
#SBATCH --time=01:00:00
#SBATCH --partition=cpu
#SBATCH --account=myaccount
# Optional for GPUs:
# SBATCH --gres=gpu:1

module load python/3.10
echo "Job $SLURM_JOB_ID running on $SLURM_JOB_NODELIST"
srun python myscript.py

Notes:
- %j expands to job ID in filenames.
- Use #SBATCH lines for Slurm options; they must appear before non-directive lines.
- Request either --mem (absolute) or --mem-per-cpu.
- Use --gres=gpu:N to request GPUs.

4) Common resource flags
- --nodes=N
- --ntasks / -n (total tasks/processes)
- --cpus-per-task (threads per task)
- --mem / --mem-per-cpu
- --time=HH:MM:SS or D-HH:MM:SS
- --partition=NAME
- --account=ACCOUNT (if accounting enforced)
- --gres=gpu:count[:type]
- --constraint=feature

5) Job arrays
- sbatch --array=1-100%10 array_job.sh
- Inside script: use $SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID to index inputs.
- %10 limits max concurrent tasks to 10.

6) Dependencies
- sbatch --dependency=afterok:12345 jobB.sh  (start jobB only if job 12345 succeeded)
- Other forms: afterany, singleton, aftercorr, afterok:job1:job2

7) Interactive examples
- Quick run (single command): srun --partition=debug --time=00:10:00 --ntasks=1 --cpus-per-task=2 bash -lc 'python -c "print(42)"'
- Start interactive shell: salloc -N1 --ntasks=4 --time=00:30:00; then srun --ntasks=4 --pty bash

8) Monitoring & troubleshooting
- squeue -u $USER -o "%.18i %.20P %.8j %.8u %.2t %.10M %.9l %.6D %R"
  (formatting shows JobID, partition, name, user, state, time, timelimit, nodes, reason)
- Pending reasons: squeue shows a reason column; for more detail: scontrol show job <jobid>
- If a job is stuck PENDING: check partition limits, QOS, account limits, dependencies, or node availability.
- For failed jobs: sacct -j <jobid> -o JobID,JobName,State,ExitCode,Elapsed,MaxRSS
- Capture stderr/stdout with --output/--error; look at those files first.

9) Environment variables worth knowing (inside job)
- SLURM_JOB_ID, SLURM_JOB_NODELIST, SLURM_NTASKS, SLURM_CPUS_ON_NODE, SLURM_NTASKS_PER_NODE, SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID

10) MPI and multi-node tips
- Use srun to launch MPI jobs (many sites integrate MPICH/OpenMPI with srun).
- Request nodes and ntasks appropriately: sbatch --nodes=4 --ntasks=128 --cpus-per-task=1
- Prefer hostfile-less MPIRUN with srun: srun --mpi=pmix ./mpi_program

11) Best practices
- Test with tiny resource requests and short times.
- Always set output/error paths to capture logs.
- Request only what you need (time, CPUs, memory) to improve scheduling.
- Use modules inside scripts to load software.
- Use job arrays for many similar tasks instead of many small sbatch submissions.
- Use checkpointing or periodic saves for long runs.
- If you need help interpretating a pending reason or limits, collect squeue and sinfo output and ask your admin.

12) Where to learn more
- Official Slurm docs: https://slurm.schedmd.com (man pages for sbatch, srun, salloc, squeue, sinfo, sacct)
- Your site’s user guide / module environment and partition names (commands above are generic; site-specific policies apply).

If you want:
- a one-page cheat sheet (printable),
- an example GPU training sbatch with common ML flags,
- an MPI example tuned for your cluster node layout,
or
- help debugging a specific job (provide job ID)
— tell me which and I’ll prepare it.

results.prompt: Slurm tutorial
results.agent_response:
Sure — here’s a concise, practical Slurm tutorial you can use as a quick reference or starter guide. Tell me if you want it focused for users, admins, GPU workflows, job arrays, or debugging and I’ll tailor it.

Basic concepts
- Controller (slurmctld): central scheduler.
- compute node (slurmd): runs tasks.
- partition: a named queue (like "gpu" or "short").
- job: a batch or interactive workload submitted to Slurm.
- step: a task-level allocation within a job (created by srun).
- QOS/account/accounting/fairshare: policy controls for priorities and limits.
- gres: generic resources (e.g., GPUs) assigned by --gres.
- reservation: a named reserved block of resources for a user/group.

Common commands (quick cheat)
- sinfo — show partition/node availability and states.
- squeue — show queued/running jobs.
- sbatch <script.sh> — submit a batch job (non-interactive).
- srun — run tasks (inside allocation or for small runs); often used inside sbatch.
- salloc — get an interactive allocation.
- scancel <jobid> — cancel a job.
- scontrol show job <id> — detailed job info.
- sacct — historical accounting (completed jobs).
- sreport — usage reports (CPU/GPU hours).
- sdiag / sprio — scheduler diagnostics and priorities.
- sshare — show fairshare usage.

Writing a basic sbatch script
Example (save as job.sh then sbatch job.sh):
#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --job-name=myjob
#SBATCH --partition=short
#SBATCH --nodes=1
#SBATCH --ntasks-per-node=4
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=2
#SBATCH --mem=8G
#SBATCH --gres=gpu:1         # request 1 GPU (if available)
#SBATCH --time=01:00:00
#SBATCH --output=job.%j.out

module load python
srun python train.py --epochs 10

Notes:
- Use CPUs/per-task vs ntasks depending on MPI vs multithreaded tasks.
- --gres=gpu:1 requests one GPU on a node that provides GPUs.
- Output file uses %j for job ID.

Interactive usage
- salloc --nodes=1 --ntasks=1 --time=00:30:00
  then run interactively:
  srun --pty bash
- Or request an interactive GPU node:
  salloc --partition=gpu --gres=gpu:1 --time=01:00:00
  then srun --pty --time=... bash

Job arrays
- Submit many similar tasks:
  #SBATCH --array=1-100%10
- Use $SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID inside your script to index inputs.
- %10 limits concurrency to 10 tasks at once.

Checking jobs and reasons
- squeue -u $USER shows your active jobs.
- squeue -j <jobid> to view a single job.
- Pending reason column (REASON or REASON field) is shown by squeue; if not, run:
  scontrol show job <jobid>
  to see the detailed reason (resources, dependency, partition limits, QOS, etc.).

Cancelling and controlling jobs
- scancel <jobid> — cancel
- scancel --user=<username> — cancel all jobs for a user (admin)
- scontrol hold <jobid> / scontrol release <jobid> — hold/release

Resources & packing tips
- Request only what you need. Over-requesting causes longer queue times.
- For multi-GPU jobs, request whole GPUs with --gres=gpu:N and ensure node has enough GPUs.
- If your code uses threads, set --cpus-per-task and export OMP_NUM_THREADS accordingly.
- For memory-heavy tasks, use --mem (per-node) or --mem-per-cpu depending on cluster config.

Debugging tips
- Do a short, small test run before scaling up.
- Check job output and the STDERR/STDOUT paths you set (by default job.%j.out).
- If pending for lack of resources, use sinfo to see partition/node idle counts.
- Use scontrol show node <nodename> to inspect node health/reasons.

#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --job-name=myjob
#SBATCH --partition=short
#SBATCH --nodes=1
#SBATCH --ntasks=1
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=4
#SBATCH --mem=8G
#SBATCH --time=01:00:00
#SBATCH --output=myjob.%j.out

module load python
srun python train.py --epochs 10

Notes on directives
- Put resource/accounting directives either as #SBATCH lines in the script or as sbatch options:
  sbatch --job-name=myjob --partition=short --cpus-per-task=4 my_job.sh
- Important options: --partition, --nodes, --ntasks, --cpus-per-task, --mem (or --mem-per-cpu), --time, --gres=gpu:1, --account, --qos, --output, --error, --mail-type/--mail-user.
- Use --gres=gpu:N to request GPUs (N = number of GPUs).
- Use --array=1-100 for array jobs; refer to $SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID in the script.
- Use --dependency=afterok:<jobid> to chain jobs.

One-line quick jobs

- See job details: scontrol show job <jobid>
- For why a job is pending, squeue shows the REASON; scontrol show job <jobid> gives more detail.

Cluster policies
- Replace partition/account names with ones valid on your cluster. If you need GPUs, confirm your cluster uses --gres=gpu or another naming convention.
- If your cluster uses accounts/QOS limits you may need --account=... or a specific QoS.

results.prompt: Slurm tutorial
results.agent_response:
Here’s a focused, practical Slurm tutorial you can use as a quick reference — covers the common commands, a job-script example, monitoring, job arrays/dependencies, interactive runs, and troubleshooting tips.

Key concepts
- Controller (slurmctld) schedules jobs. Compute nodes run steps.
- Jobs vs. steps: a job is an allocation; steps (srun) run tasks inside it.
- Partitions group nodes (like queues). QOS, accounts, and limits control usage.
- Resources: nodes, CPUs (tasks & cpus-per-task), memory, GPUs (GRES).

Common commands
- sbatch <script> — submit a batch job (non-interactive).
- srun [args] command — run a job step (inside an allocation or under sbatch/salloc).
- salloc [options] — get an interactive allocation.
- squeue — view queued/running jobs; use filters (e.g., squeue -u $USER).
- sinfo — view partition and node state.
- scancel JOBID — cancel a job.
- scontrol show job JOBID — detailed job info.
- sacct — accounting/history of completed jobs.
- sstat JOBID — runtime stats for a running job.
- scontrol show config / scontrol ping — controller diagnostics.

Minimal sbatch job script
Example: run a Python program on 1 node with 4 CPUs and 1 GPU for 2 hours.

#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --job-name=myjob
#SBATCH --output=slurm-%j.out
#SBATCH --error=slurm-%j.err
#SBATCH --time=02:00:00           # HH:MM:SS
#SBATCH --partition=gpu
#SBATCH --nodes=1
#SBATCH --ntasks=1                # number of tasks/processes
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=4
#SBATCH --mem=16G                 # memory per node (or use --mem-per-cpu)
#SBATCH --gres=gpu:1              # request 1 GPU
#SBATCH --account=your_account
#SBATCH --mail-type=END,FAIL
#SBATCH --mail-user=you@example.com

module load python/3.10
# Use srun to launch the job step (recommended for MPI or multi-rank)
srun python train.py --epochs 10

Notes on resource directives
- --nodes vs --ntasks: nodes = physical nodes; ntasks = number of MPI ranks or processes.
- --cpus-per-task: threads per task (e.g., for OpenMP).
- --mem (per node) vs --mem-per-cpu.
- --gres=gpu:N to request GPUs (N integer). Some clusters use different gres names; check sinfo or docs.
- Time limits matter: jobs killed at time limit. Be conservative but accurate.
- Output files: %j expands to jobid (slurm-%j.out).

Interactive jobs
- salloc --nodes=1 --ntasks=1 --time=01:00:00 --gres=gpu:1
  then run srun --pty bash to get a prompt on an allocated node.
- srun --partition=debug --pty bash -i (if cluster allows direct srun interactive sessions)

Job arrays
- sbatch --array=1-100%10 array_script.sh
- Use $SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID inside the script to get the index.
- %10 limits concurrency to 10 array tasks at once.

Job dependencies
- sbatch --dependency=afterok:12345 job2.sh  (run job2 only if job 12345 succeeds)
- Other dependency types: afterany, aftercorr, singleton, expand, etc.

Monitoring and debugging
- squeue -u $USER -o "%.18i %.9P %.35j %.8u %.2t %.10M %R"  (custom format: jobid, partition, name, user, state, time, reason)
- squeue -j JOBID  (check specific job)
- scontrol show job JOBID  (detailed fields like Reason, State, TRES)
- sacct -j JOBID --format=JobID,JobName,State,ExitCode,Elapsed  (history after job finishes)
- sstat -j JOBID  (live stats for running jobs)
- sinfo -s  (partition summary)
- sinfo -N -l  (node-level details)

Common reasons jobs stay pending
- No free nodes in requested partition or with requested features.
- Insufficient resources requested (e.g., requested more GPUs than any single node has).
- User or account QOS/limits reached (job or cluster fairshare limits).
- Reservation is active (jobs may be blocked or favored).
- Job’s constraints (node features, gres, or node list) don’t match available nodes.
To inspect: squeue (check REASON column) then sinfo (see partition/node availability), and scontrol show job JOBID for full reason text.

MPI and multi-process jobs
- Use srun for MPI-launch integration (srun handles binding, placement). Example:
  sbatch with --ntasks=16 and within script: srun --mpi=pmix ./my_mpi_program
- For mpirun/mpiexec, cluster may still require srun or be configured to allow mpirun under the allocation—check local guidance.

Best practices
- Test interactively with small resources and a short time first.
- Right-size CPU/memory/gpu requests; over-requesting wastes queue slots and delays scheduling.
- Put module loads and environment setup in the script so the batch job environment matches interactive tests.
- Use checkpoints or save intermediate results for long jobs.
- Keep output and error files organized (use --output/--error or redirect).
- Prefer srun inside sbatch scripts to start tasks (ensures Slurm tracks steps).

Useful examples and formats
- Check a single job: squeue -j JOBID; if missing, check sacct -j JOBID to see historical records.
- See node states and GPU counts: sinfo -Nl or sinfo --format="%n %T %c %G" (cluster dependent).
- Cancel all your pending jobs: scancel -u $USER (destructive — be careful).

Where to read more
- sbatch, srun, salloc, squeue, sinfo, scontrol, sacct pages in the official Slurm docs (slurm.schedmd.com) — they have complete option lists and examples.

If you want, I can:
- Show a ready-to-use job script template for your workload (MPI / multi-GPU / single-GPU / CPU-only).
- Walk through why one of your jobs is pending or failed — if so, tell me the job ID and I’ll show the commands to inspect it.

results.prompt: How do I write a good Slurm batch script?
results.agent_response:
Good question — a clear, well‑written Slurm batch script makes jobs easier to run, debug, and reproduce. Below are practical guidelines, common pitfalls, and several compact example scripts you can adapt.

Essential structure
- Start with a shell shebang (#!/bin/bash).
- Put SBATCH directives near the top (either as comments with #SBATCH or passed to sbatch on the command line).
- Load modules / activate environments.
- Set up working and scratch directories, stage input, build environment.
- Run workload with srun (or appropriate MPI launcher / singularity / python, etc.).
- Clean up and move outputs back to persistent storage.

Common SBATCH directives (most useful)
- --job-name=NAME
- --output=path/to/out.%j.log  (use %j for jobid)
- --error=path/to/err.%j.log  (or combine with --output)
- --partition=PARTITION
- --nodes=N
- --ntasks=NTASKS
- --cpus-per-task=CPUS
- --mem=MEM  or --mem-per-cpu=MEM
- --gres=gpu:TYPE:COUNT  (e.g., --gres=gpu:1)
- --time=DD-HH:MM:SS  (or HH:MM:SS)
- --account=ACCOUNT or --qos=QOS
- --mail-type=END,FAIL,BEGIN  and --mail-user=you@example.com
- --array=1-100  (for array jobs)
- --dependency=afterok:1234 (job chaining)

Good scripting practices
- Minimal, explicit resource requests: ask for what you need (helps scheduling and avoids wastage).
- Use srun for parallel MPI/OMP tasks rather than plain mpirun when possible — srun integrates with Slurm allocation and cgroups.
- Prefer --mem-per-cpu when threads per task vary; use --mem for fixed per‑node memory.
- Always cd to a known working directory (e.g., cd $SLURM_SUBMIT_DIR or $HOME/project).
- Use set -euo pipefail (or at least set -e) to fail early on errors.
- Use trap to catch SIGTERM and save state/cleanup if your job may be preempted.
- Keep logs per job (use %j in output file names).
- Staging: copy large input to node-local scratch (e.g., /scratch/$USER/$SLURM_JOB_ID), run there, then copy outputs back to shared filesystem.
- Do a small short test run locally or with reduced resources before full submission.
- Use descriptive job-name and directories so outputs are self-documenting.

Environment & reproducibility
- Load specific module versions or explicit container images (Singularity/Apptainer). Example:
  module load python/3.10
  source /path/to/venv/bin/activate
  or
  singularity exec image.sif python script.py
- Record the environment (module list, python -V, pip freeze) to output logs.

Monitoring and debugging
- squeue -j JOBID or squeue -u $USER to see queue status.
- sacct -j JOBID --format=JobID,State,Elapsed,ExitCode for postmortem info.
- sstat -j JOBID for runtime statistics of running jobs.
- Use sbatch --test-only to validate resource directives without actually starting a job (if available).

Signal handling example (catching SIGTERM)
- trap 'echo "SIGTERM caught; copying logs"; rsync -av $SCRATCH/out $HOME/results; exit 0' TERM

Useful environment variables provided by Slurm
- SLURM_JOB_ID, SLURM_JOB_NODELIST, SLURM_NTASKS, SLURM_CPUS_ON_NODE, SLURM_JOB_NAME, SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID

Examples
1) Simple single-node CPU job
#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --job-name=hello
#SBATCH --output=logs/hello.%j.out
#SBATCH --error=logs/hello.%j.err
#SBATCH --partition=standard
#SBATCH --nodes=1
#SBATCH --ntasks=1
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=4
#SBATCH --time=01:00:00
#SBATCH --mem=8G

set -euo pipefail
cd $SLURM_SUBMIT_DIR
module load python/3.10
python train.py --threads $SLURM_CPUS_ON_NODE

2) MPI job (multi-node)
#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --job-name=mpi-run
#SBATCH --output=logs/mpi.%j.out
#SBATCH --nodes=4
#SBATCH --ntasks-per-node=16
#SBATCH --time=02:00:00
#SBATCH --partition=bigmem

set -e
cd $SLURM_SUBMIT_DIR
module load mpi/openmpi-x.y
srun --mpi=pmix ./my_mpi_executable   # srun will launch across the allocated nodes

3) GPU job
#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --job-name=gpu-train
#SBATCH --output=logs/gpu.%j.out
#SBATCH --gres=gpu:1
#SBATCH --ntasks=1
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=8
#SBATCH --time=06:00:00
#SBATCH --partition=gpu

set -euo pipefail
cd $SLURM_SUBMIT_DIR
module load cuda/12.0
module load cudnn
source venv/bin/activate
python train_gpu.py --batch-size 64

4) Array job (parallelizing parameter sweeps)
#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --job-name=array-job
#SBATCH --output=logs/array.%A_%a.out
#SBATCH --array=1-50
#SBATCH --time=00:30:00
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=2

set -e
params_file=params.txt
param=$(sed -n "${SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID}p" $params_file)
python run_experiment.py --param $param

Best practices & gotchas
- Time estimates: underestimate time and your job will be killed when it expires; overestimate and you may wait in queue or be billed for more. Do short profiling runs to get realistic times.
- Filesystem I/O: avoid many small writes to shared filesystems from many tasks; use node-local scratch for heavy I/O, then rsync back.
- GPUs: don’t assume device IDs; set CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES if necessary, but prefer Slurm’s allocation (CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES is often set by the cluster).
- Memory vs. swap: Slurm enforces requested memory via cgroups; exceeding it often causes OOM kill. Request adequate memory.
- Interactive debugging: srun --pty --nodes=1 --ntasks=1 --time=01:00:00 bash (or use cluster-provided interactive allocation tools) to debug interactively.
- Check cluster-specific policies: partition names, gres labels, QoS, max time limits, account fields differ by cluster.

When to use sbatch vs srun
- sbatch submits a batch script to the scheduler.
- srun runs a command inside an allocation (used inside a batch script or inside an interactive allocation). Do not use srun to submit batch scripts.

Short checklist before submitting
- Small test run passes.
- Output paths and logging are set (including stderr).
- Resource requests (nodes, cpus, mem, gpus) match actual needs.
- Environment/modules specified explicitly.
- Data staged or accessible from nodes.
- Cleanup paths and copy-back steps in place.

If you want, tell me:
- the kind of job you run (serial, MPI, GPU, Python, container),
- sample resource needs (CPUs, GPUs, memory, nodes),
and I’ll draft a ready-to-submit batch script tailored to your cluster style.

results.prompt: Slurm tutorial
results.agent_response:
Good — here’s a concise, practical Slurm tutorial you can use as a quick reference and to get started submitting and debugging jobs.

1) Key concepts
- Controller and compute nodes: slurmctld (controller) schedules jobs onto compute nodes.
- Partition: grouping of nodes (like a queue). You request a partition with --partition.
- Job vs step: a job (sbatch) can contain one or more steps (srun creates steps). The batch script is a job; srun runs work inside the job allocation.
- Resources: nodes, CPUs (cores), tasks, cpus-per-task, memory, GPUs (gres), time limit (--time).
- QOS / accounts / limits: policies that may restrict runtime, priority, or concurrent jobs.

2) Common commands (quick)
- sbatch myjob.sh — submit a batch script (noninteractive).
- srun ... — run a step (inside an allocation) or directly in a job script.
- salloc — get an interactive allocation (useful for debugging).
- squeue — show the active queue (pending/running jobs).
- sinfo — show partitions and node availability.
- scontrol show job <jobid> — detailed job info.
- scontrol show node <nodename> — detailed node info.
- sacct — accounting/history for completed jobs.
- scancel <jobid> — cancel a job.
- sstat -j <jobid> — live stats for running job steps.
- sreport / sshare — usage/fairshare reports.

3) Minimal sbatch script (example)
#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --job-name=myjob
#SBATCH --partition=regular
#SBATCH --nodes=1
#SBATCH --ntasks=4
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=1
#SBATCH --time=01:00:00
#SBATCH --mem=8G
#SBATCH --output=slurm-%j.out
module load python
srun python train.py

Notes:
- Lines beginning with #SBATCH are directives parsed by Slurm.
- Default output file is slurm-%j.out where %j expands to the jobid.
- Use module load (or your environment system) inside the script before running your program.

4) Requesting GPUs
- Example: #SBATCH --gres=gpu:1
- Also consider memory, CPUs, and partition constraints when using GPUs.

5) Job arrays
- Submit many similar tasks efficiently: sbatch --array=1-100%10 my_array.sh
- Inside script use $SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID to pick the task’s index.
- Placeholders in file names: %A = master jobid, %a = array index, %j = jobid.

6) Dependencies
- Wait for a job to finish before starting another:
  --depend=afterok:<jobid>  (start only if <jobid> completed OK)
  --depend=afterany:<jobid> (start after completion regardless of exit)
  Example: sbatch --depend=afterok:12345 job2.sh

7) Interactive debugging
- salloc --nodes=1 --ntasks=1 --time=00:30:00 --partition=debug
- then run srun or launch an interactive shell inside the allocation.

8) Inspecting the queue and diagnosing pending jobs
- squeue -u $USER  (your jobs)
- squeue -j <jobid> (single job)
- If a job is PENDING, squeue usually shows a REASON column (e.g., Resources, ReqNodeNotAvail, QOSMaxJobs).
- Common reasons and quick fixes:
  - Resources: no free nodes with requested resources — try fewer resources or different partition, or wait.
  - ReqNodeNotAvail / NodeDown: requested nodes are offline — pick a different partition or contact admin.
  - Priority: low priority / fairshare — wait or request a higher QOS (if allowed).
  - Dependency: job depends on another job that hasn’t finished — check the dependency target.
- For detailed pending reason: scontrol show job <jobid>.

9) Viewing job output and errors
- Standard output and error are written to the file you set with --output and --error (or together with --output=slurm-%j.out).
- Check slurm-<jobid>.out for program output and immediate errors.

10) Accounting and job history
- sacct -j <jobid> --format=JobID,JobName,State,ExitCode,Elapsed,ReqMem
- sacct -u username --starttime=2024-01-01 (get historical usage).
- Use sreport / sshare for cluster-wide or fairshare usage summaries.

11) Performance monitoring (running jobs)
- sstat -j <jobid>.batch or steps: shows CPU/memory I/O for running steps (not for finished jobs).
- Use node-level tools (top, nvidia-smi) from within an allocation for deeper runtime profiling.

12) Cancel, hold, requeue
- scancel <jobid> — cancel a job.
- scontrol hold <jobid> / scontrol release <jobid> — place a hold / release it (admin or allowed users).
- For bulk operations (cancel all jobs by user/partition), scancel supports filters (admins typically do this).

13) Best practices
- Start small: request minimal resources and short time while debugging.
- Set realistic time limits; jobs killed for exceeding time will still count as failures.
- Use --output and --error to capture logs and include jobid in filenames for traceability.
- Use job arrays for parameter sweeps rather than many separate submits.
- Tag jobs with --job-name so you can identify them in squeue/sacct.
- Test interactively with salloc before scaling to many nodes.

14) Troubleshooting checklist (if job fails or is stuck)
- squeue -j <jobid> to check state/reason.
- scontrol show job <jobid> for details (reservation, node constraints, gres).
- Check slurm-<jobid>.out and application logs.
- sacct -j <jobid> to see exit codes and why it ended.
- If pending due to resources, run sinfo to confirm partition/node availability.
- If node failures or drained nodes appear, run sinfo -R or contact cluster admin.

15) Useful examples
- GPU training job:
#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --job-name=gpu_train
#SBATCH --partition=gpu
#SBATCH --gres=gpu:1
#SBATCH --nodes=1
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=4
#SBATCH --mem=32G
#SBATCH --time=08:00:00
module load cuda
srun python train_gpu.py

- Job array example (index-based):
#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --job-name=array_demo
#SBATCH --array=1-10
#SBATCH --output=out_%a.txt
python process.py --task $SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID

If you want, I can:
- Walk through writing a sbatch for one of your real scripts,
- Inspect your cluster’s current partitions and nodes (sinfo) or your queue (squeue) — tell me which read you want,
- Or show detailed sbatch options for advanced features (heterogeneous jobs, burst buffers, QOS). Which would you like next?

results.prompt: How do I submit a job?
results.agent_response:
Short answer — create a batch script with #SBATCH directives, then run sbatch <script>. Below are the steps, common options, and a minimal example.

1) Create a batch script
- Start with a shell shebang: #!/bin/bash
- Add #SBATCH lines for the scheduler options (time, nodes, cpus, memory, gpus, job name, output files, etc.)
- Put the commands you want to run (module load, mpirun, python, etc.) after the SBATCH header.

Common sbatch options (examples)
- --job-name=NAME or #SBATCH --job-name=NAME
- --time=HH:MM:SS or days-HH:MM:SS (set max runtime)
- --nodes=N (number of nodes)
- --ntasks=N (total MPI tasks)
- --cpus-per-task=N (threads per task)
- --mem=4G or --mem-per-cpu=2G (memory)
- --gres=gpu:1 (request GPUs; e.g., gpu:2)
- --partition=partition_name (which partition/queue)
- --output=slurm-%j.out (stdout; %j expands to jobid)
- --error=slurm-%j.err (stderr)
- --mail-type=END,FAIL --mail-user=you@domain (email notifications)
- --array=1-100 (array jobs)
- --export=ALL or --export=NONE (environment export)

Minimal example (save as myjob.sh)
#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --job-name=myjob
#SBATCH --time=02:00:00
#SBATCH --partition=standard
#SBATCH --nodes=1
#SBATCH --ntasks=1
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=4
#SBATCH --mem=8G
#SBATCH --output=job-%j.out
#SBATCH --error=job-%j.err

module load python/3.10
echo "Job $SLURM_JOB_ID running on $(hostname)"
python train.py --epochs 10

2) Submit the job
- sbatch myjob.sh
- sbatch will print the assigned job id, e.g. Submitted batch job 12345

3) Monitor and manage jobs
- squeue -u yourusername (list your queued/running jobs)
- squeue -j 12345 (check a specific job)
- scontrol show job 12345 (detailed job info)
- sacct -j 12345 (after job completes, accounting info)
- scancel 12345 (cancel a job)

4) Useful extras
- Array jobs: add #SBATCH --array=1-10 and use $SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID in the script to index inputs.
- GPUs: request with #SBATCH --gres=gpu:<count> and be sure the partition has GPUs (ask or check sinfo).
- Interactive runs: use salloc or srun for interactive allocations (salloc --time=01:00 --gres=gpu:1; srun --pty bash).
- Output files: use %j in --output/--error to include job ID.
- Environment: SLURM sets variables like SLURM_JOB_ID, SLURM_NODELIST, etc.

If you want, tell me:
- whether you need CPU or GPU resources, or
- a sample command/script you want to run,
and I can give a ready-to-submit script tuned to your needs.

results.prompt: Slurm tutorial
results.agent_response:
Good — here’s a compact, practical Slurm tutorial you can use as a quick reference and starter guide.

Core concepts
- Controller (slurmctld): scheduler daemon.
- Nodes: compute machines; grouped into partitions (queues).
- Job: a workload submitted to Slurm (batch job, interactive allocation, or step).
- Allocation vs. job step: sbatch creates a batch job (runs a script). salloc allocates resources for interactive use. srun launches tasks/steps (can be used inside an allocation or a batch script).
- TRES: tracked resources (CPUs, memory, GPUs, licenses).

Common commands (quick)
- Submit a batch job: sbatch myscript.sh
- Request an interactive allocation: salloc --nodes=1 --time=01:00:00
- Run a task immediately (within allocation or to get allocation): srun -n4 ./myprog
- See queued/running jobs: squeue [-u $USER]
- View partitions/nodes: sinfo
- View job details: scontrol show job <jobid>
- View historical/completed jobs: sacct -j <jobid>
- Cancel a job: scancel <jobid>
- Real-time stats for running job: sstat -j <jobid>

Basic sbatch script (single-node GPU example)
#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --job-name=my_gpu_job
#SBATCH --partition=gpu
#SBATCH --nodes=1
#SBATCH --ntasks=1
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=8
#SBATCH --gres=gpu:1               # request 1 GPU
#SBATCH --mem=32G
#SBATCH --time=02:00:00
#SBATCH --output=logs/%x.%j.out
#SBATCH --error=logs/%x.%j.err

module load cuda/11.8
source ~/envs/myenv/bin/activate
srun python train.py --epochs 10

Notes:
- #SBATCH lines are parsed by sbatch; options can also be given on the sbatch command line.
- Use --gres=gpu:<count> to request GPUs.
- --cpus-per-task is for CPU threads per task (useful for multi-threaded apps).
- Use --mem (per node) or --mem-per-cpu depending on cluster config.

Interactive use patterns
- Quick interactive run: salloc --nodes=1 --time=01:00:00 --gres=gpu:1
  then run srun -n1 --gres=gpu:1 python -i
- For quick commands you can do: srun --pty --nodes=1 --ntasks=1 bash

Job arrays
- Syntax: sbatch --array=1-100%10 array_script.sh
- Inside your script: use $SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID to vary input per task.
- %10 limits concurrency to 10 at once.

Dependencies (run-after)
- sbatch --dependency=afterok:<jobid> next_job.sh
- Other forms: afterany, aftercorr, afterok:job1:job2, etc.

Monitoring & debugging
- squeue -u $USER shows job state (PENDING, RUNNING, COMPLETED, FAILED).
- If PENDING, see the pending reason column (REASON) in squeue; for more detail: scontrol show job <jobid>.
- For completed jobs, use sacct -j <jobid> to get ExitCode, Elapsed, Timelimit info.
- sstat -j <jobid> gives live resource usage for running jobs.
- sbatch --output and --error (or combined with --output=...) capture stdout/stderr for post-mortem.

Common resource options
- --partition or -p
- --nodes, --ntasks, --ntasks-per-node
- --cpus-per-task
- --mem or --mem-per-cpu
- --gres=gpu:<N> (GPUs)
- --time=HH:MM:SS
- --qos (if configured)
- --account (if required by site policy)

Environment variables useful inside jobs
- SLURM_JOB_ID: job ID
- SLURM_JOB_NODELIST: allocated nodes
- SLURM_NTASKS, SLURM_PROCID, SLURM_CPUS_ON_NODE
- For arrays: SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID

MPI and parallel jobs
- Use srun to launch MPI tasks (srun often wraps mpirun).
- Example: srun -n 32 --cpus-per-task=2 ./mpi_program
- Ensure your MPI is compiled with the cluster’s network libraries.

Best practices
- Start with a small, short test job to verify environment and modules.
- Request only what you need (memory, CPUs, GPUs) — over-requesting hurts scheduling and can delay your job.
- Use checkpoints or periodic saving for long jobs.
- Put long-running outputs and logs into a persistent shared filesystem.
- Use job arrays instead of many small sbatch submissions where possible.
- Use output paths with job names and IDs (e.g., logs/%x.%j.out) to avoid collisions.

Troubleshooting tips
- Job pending with reason “Priority” or “Resources”: use sinfo to see partition node counts and availability.
- If your job fails immediately, check stderr/stdout paths, and then sacct -j <jobid> --format=JobID,State,ExitCode for exit code.
- For unclear pending reasons: scontrol show job <jobid>.
- For node issues (down/drain), run sinfo -R or ask admins.

Useful admin/inspection commands (what to run when)
- sinfo — partition/node availability and states
- squeue — live queue
- scontrol show job <jobid> — detailed job config and priority info
- sacct -S <starttime> -u <user> — historical accounting
- sstat -j <jobid> — running job resource stats

Where to learn more
- Official Slurm docs: https://slurm.schedmd.com (good refs: sbatch, srun, salloc, squeue, job_array)
- Your site’s local docs / module environment and policies (account/QoS limits, partitions, usage rules).

- Generate a ready-to-submit sbatch script for a specific program (tell me CPUs, mem, gpus, time).
- Walk through submitting and diagnosing a particular job (give me the job script or job ID).
- Show examples for MPI, TensorFlow/PyTorch GPU jobs, or job arrays with file-splitting.

results.prompt: How do I write a good Slurm batch script?
results.agent_response:
Good question — a clear, minimal, and reproducible sbatch script saves time and headaches. Below is a compact checklist of what to include, why it matters, and three practical example scripts (simple CPU, GPU, and MPI + job-array). Use the parts you need.

Quick checklist (order matters)
- Put all #SBATCH directives at the top of the file before any non-comment line — Slurm stops parsing directives after the first non-comment/non-whitespace line.
- Request the correct resources: partition, time, CPUs, memory, GPUs (gres), ntasks / ntasks-per-node, cpus-per-task, qos, account.
- Give a job name (--job-name) and deterministic output/error paths (--output, --error) using %j or %A_%a for arrays.
- Set a realistic time limit. Jobs killed for exceeding time are harder to recover.
- Set environment for reproducibility: module loads, conda/venv activation, print environment/module list to the log.
- Use srun to launch tasks (prefer srun for Slurm-built MPI/parallel jobs).
- Handle errors: set -e, trap to capture exit status, and save logs/diagnostics.
- Tune memory and CPU mapping: cpus-per-task, OMP_NUM_THREADS, --hint, --exclusive if needed.
- For GPUs: request gres=gpu:<count> and bind CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES or let your container handle it.
- Use job arrays for many similar tasks; use --array with %a environment variable.
- Use dependencies (--depend=afterok:JOBID) for workflows.
- Use checkpointing or output snapshots for long runs.
- Test interactively on a small allocation before large submission.

Good sbatch header fields (common)
- #SBATCH --job-name=NAME
- #SBATCH --partition=partition_name
- #SBATCH --account=account_name
- #SBATCH --qos=name
- #SBATCH --time=HH:MM:SS
- #SBATCH --nodes=N
- #SBATCH --ntasks=NTASKS
- #SBATCH --ntasks-per-node=NTASKS_PER_NODE
- #SBATCH --cpus-per-task=CPUS
- #SBATCH --mem=4G (or --mem-per-cpu=2G)
- #SBATCH --gres=gpu:1
- #SBATCH --output=logs/%x-%j.out
- #SBATCH --error=logs/%x-%j.err
- #SBATCH --mail-type=BEGIN,END,FAIL --mail-user=you@example.com
- #SBATCH --array=1-100%20 (for job arrays, limit concurrency with %)

Runtime environment best practices
- Load modules once (module purge; module load ...). Save module list (module list > $SLURM_JOB_ID.modules) for reproducibility.
- Set thread/environment variables for hybrid MPI+OpenMP:
  - export OMP_NUM_THREADS=$SLURM_CPUS_PER_TASK
  - export MKL_NUM_THREADS=$OMP_NUM_THREADS
- Use srun to launch processes so Slurm handles cpu/gpu binding:
  - srun -n $SLURM_NTASKS ./my_mpi_app
- Use containers (Singularity/Apptainer) for consistent environments:
  - singularity exec --nv my_image.sif python train.py
- Capture exit codes and exit non-zero on failure:
  - set -euo pipefail
  - trap 'rc=$?; echo "Exit $rc"; exit $rc' EXIT

Logging and debugging
- Use meaningful file names: --output=logs/%x.%j.out
- Print key diagnostics at start: date, hostname, /proc/cpuinfo, nvidia-smi, free -h, env | sort
- For intermittent failures, save stderr/stdout and small checkpoints.
- When debugging, ask for a small interactive allocation (salloc) or request very short --time and low resources.

Portability tips
- Avoid hardcoding absolute module names or path-dependent commands.
- Use SBATCH variables and environment variables instead of magic numbers.
- Use %j (jobid) and %x (jobname) in output filenames to avoid collisions.

Examples

1) Simple single-node CPU job
#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --job-name=hello_cpu
#SBATCH --partition=normal
#SBATCH --time=01:00:00
#SBATCH --nodes=1
#SBATCH --ntasks=1
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=4
#SBATCH --mem=8G
#SBATCH --output=logs/%x-%j.out
#SBATCH --error=logs/%x-%j.err

set -euo pipefail
echo "Job: $SLURM_JOB_ID, started at $(date)"
module purge
module load python/3.10
module list > logs/${SLURM_JOB_ID}.modules

export OMP_NUM_THREADS=$SLURM_CPUS_PER_TASK
python my_script.py --threads $OMP_NUM_THREADS

2) GPU training job (single node, multi-GPU)
#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --job-name=train_gpu
#SBATCH --partition=gpu
#SBATCH --time=12:00:00
#SBATCH --nodes=1
#SBATCH --ntasks=1
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=8
#SBATCH --gres=gpu:2
#SBATCH --mem=64G
#SBATCH --output=logs/%x-%j.out

set -euo pipefail
echo "Job: $SLURM_JOB_ID on $(hostname) GPUs:"
nvidia-smi
module purge
module load cuda/12.0
source ~/envs/myenv/bin/activate
python train.py --gpus 2 --workers 8

3) MPI job with node packing and job-array example
MPI launcher (single MPI job)
#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --job-name=mpi_run
#SBATCH --partition=mpi
#SBATCH --time=02:00:00
#SBATCH --nodes=4
#SBATCH --ntasks-per-node=16
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=1
#SBATCH --output=logs/%x-%j.out

set -euo pipefail
module purge
module load openmpi
srun --mpi=pmix -n $SLURM_NTASKS ./my_mpi_executable

Job array (many parameter sweep tasks)
#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --job-name=sweep
#SBATCH --array=1-100%10
#SBATCH --time=00:30:00
#SBATCH --ntasks=1
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=2
#SBATCH --mem=4G
#SBATCH --output=logs/%x-%A_%a.out

set -euo pipefail
PARAM_FILE=params.txt
PARAM=$(sed -n "${SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID}p" $PARAM_FILE)
echo "Running index $SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID param=$PARAM"
python run_exp.py --param "$PARAM"

Other useful tips
- Conservatively estimate resources; under-requesting memory leads to OOM kills with little trace.
- For important long jobs, consider --requeue and checkpointing so they can resume after preemption.
- Use --exclusive if you need whole-node exclusivity.
- Keep scripts idempotent and reproducible: don’t change working files in place without backups.
- For complex workflows, use a workflow manager (Nextflow, Snakemake) or Slurm dependencies.

If you want, I can:
- Review one of your existing scripts and point out improvements (paste it here).
- Generate a tailored template for your workload (MPI, GPU deep learning, HPC pipeline, etc.).

results.prompt: Slurm tutorial
results.agent_response:
Below is a compact, practical Slurm tutorial covering core concepts, common commands, example batch scripts, job arrays/dependencies, monitoring/troubleshooting, and best practices. Tell me if you want a deeper dive on any area or examples tailored to your cluster (CPU vs GPU, MPI vs single-node).

1) Big-picture concepts
- Slurm is a job scheduler that manages partitions (queues), nodes, and jobs. Users submit jobs (batch or interactive) which are queued and scheduled onto nodes.
- Key entities: job, step (task within a job), node, partition, QOS, account, reservation.
- Resource requests drive scheduling: nodes, CPUs, memory, GPUs (gres), walltime, and constraints.

2) Important commands (quick reference)
- sinfo — show partition/node availability and states.
  Example: sinfo
- squeue — view queued/running jobs.
  Example: squeue -u $USER or squeue -o "%.18i %.9P %.8j %.8u %.2t %.10M %.6D %R"
- sbatch — submit a batch/script job (non-interactive).
  Example: sbatch myscript.sh
- srun — start tasks (MPI/parallel tasks) inside an allocation or interactively.
  Example (inside sbatch): srun -n 16 ./my_mpi_prog
- salloc — get an interactive allocation (useful for debugging/interactive runs).
  Example: salloc --nodes=1 --ntasks=4 --time=01:00:00
- scancel — cancel jobs.
  Example: scancel 12345
- scontrol show job <id> — show detailed job fields and pending reason.
- sacct — accounting/history of completed jobs.
  Example: sacct -j 12345 --format=JobID,JobName,State,ExitCode,Elapsed
- sstat — runtime stats for running job steps (CPU%, memory).
- sreport / sshare / sprio — reporting, fairshare, priority diagnostics.
- scontrol — controller operations (admins): hold/release jobs, update job limits, node actions (admins only).

3) Example sbatch script (simple CPU job)
#!/bin/sh
#SBATCH --job-name=myjob
#SBATCH --output=slurm-%j.out
#SBATCH --error=slurm-%j.err
#SBATCH --partition=short
#SBATCH --nodes=1
#SBATCH --ntasks=4
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=2
#SBATCH --mem=8G
#SBATCH --time=02:00:00
# load modules, set env
module load python
srun python train.py --epochs 10

Notes:
- #SBATCH directives are parsed only until the first non-comment, non-whitespace line.
- Output file slurm-%j.out (%j → jobid).
- Use --mem for total memory on node or --mem-per-cpu.
- For GPUs: add #SBATCH --gres=gpu:1 and a GPU partition if required.

4) Example GPU sbatch snippet
#SBATCH --job-name=gpu_train
#SBATCH --partition=gpu
#SBATCH --gres=gpu:2
#SBATCH --nodes=1
#SBATCH --ntasks=1
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=8
#SBATCH --mem=32G
#SBATCH --time=08:00:00
srun python train_gpu.py

5) Job arrays and dependencies
- Job array: submit many similar tasks:
  sbatch --array=1-100%10 array_job.sh
  Inside script use $SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID.
- Dependencies: chain jobs so B starts after A completes:
  sbatch --dependency=afterok:12345 next_job.sh
  Other dependency types: afterany, aftercorr, afterok:job1:job2,...

6) Interactive workflows
- Quick interactive run on a compute node: salloc --nodes=1 --ntasks=1 --time=01:00:00 then srun --pty bash
- For interactive MPI debugging, allocate nodes first with salloc then run srun -n <procs> ./prog.

7) Monitoring and debugging

results.prompt: Show me a safe sbatch script pattern
results.agent_response:
Below is a compact, practical, and safe sbatch script pattern you can adapt. It demonstrates defensive bash settings, resource-aware environment setup, robust staging and cleanup, signal handling for preemption, and safe use of srun. Replace values (partition, time, memory, modules, commands, staging paths) with your cluster-specific choices.

#!/usr/bin/env bash
#SBATCH --job-name=myjob               # short name
#SBATCH --output=%x-%j.out             # %x=job-name %j=jobid
#SBATCH --error=%x-%j.err
#SBATCH --time=02:00:00                # walltime
#SBATCH --partition=compute
#SBATCH --nodes=1
#SBATCH --ntasks=1
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=4
#SBATCH --mem=16G
#SBATCH --gres=gpu:1                   # remove if not a GPU job
#SBATCH --mail-type=FAIL,END
#SBATCH --mail-user=you@example.com

set -euo pipefail                       # fail fast, catch unset vars
IFS=$'\n\t'
ulimit -c 0                             # don't produce core files (cluster policy)
umask 0022

# Useful Slurm env vars:
echo "Job $SLURM_JOB_NAME ($SLURM_JOB_ID) on $(hostname) nodes:$SLURM_NODELIST"
echo "Started: $(date)"

# Configure threaded libs
export OMP_NUM_THREADS=${SLURM_CPUS_PER_TASK:-1}
export MKL_NUM_THREADS=${OMP_NUM_THREADS}

# Create per-job workspace on fast local storage if available
SCRATCH=${SCRATCH:-/scratch/$USER}
WORKDIR="$SCRATCH/$USER/$SLURM_JOB_ID"
mkdir -p "$WORKDIR"
cd "$WORKDIR"

# Load modules / software
module purge
module load python/3.10 cuda/12.0   # example; use your cluster modules

# Cleanup and signal handling
cleanup() {
  rc=${1:-$?}
  echo "Job cleanup (exit $rc) at $(date)"
  # stage out results back to persistent storage
  rsync -av --progress ./results/ /home/$USER/results/$SLURM_JOB_ID/ || echo "rsync failed"
  # remove large local tmp if desired:
  # rm -rf "$WORKDIR"
  exit $rc
}

on_term() {
  echo "Received SIGTERM or preemption signal at $(date) - try to checkpoint"
  # perform lightweight checkpoint: flush logs, save state files, etc.
  # do not rely on long-running operations here
  cleanup 143   # 128+15=SIGTERM
}

trap 'on_term' TERM INT
trap 'cleanup 0' EXIT

# Optional: create a small runtime log
exec > >(tee -a "$WORKDIR/job.log") 2>&1

# Example safety checks
if [ ! -d "$WORKDIR" ]; then
  echo "Failed to create workdir $WORKDIR"; exit 1
fi

# Run the real work under srun so Slurm launches tasks properly
echo "Running job command at $(date)"
srun --cpu-bind=cores my_program --threads $OMP_NUM_THREADS --out ./results/out.txt

# Normal exit triggers cleanup trap
echo "Finished: $(date)"
exit 0

Notes and best practices:
- Use #SBATCH directives for the canonical settings; prefer explicit CPU/memory/gres values rather than overcommitting.
- Use set -euo pipefail and a trap-based cleanup to avoid leaving partial state and to stage results back to persistent storage.
- Use srun (not plain exe) so Slurm tracks your tasks and handles signals/affinity correctly.
- Keep SIGTERM handlers short and reliable (save small checkpoints); clusters often send SIGTERM shortly before kill.
- Use local fast storage (TMPDIR, $SCRATCH) for heavy I/O, and rsync results back at the end so network filesystems don't slow the run.
- For job arrays, use #SBATCH --array=1-100%20 and consult SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID; limit concurrent tasks with % to avoid overloading shared data.
- Avoid long global cleanup in SIGTERM; do minimal checkpoint then exit. Requeueing from within the job may require permissions—ask your admin.
- Include meaningful --output/--error naming (with %j/%x) so logs are easy to find.
- Test interactively or with a short time limit before submitting long runs.

If you want, I can produce a variant tailored to: GPUs (multi-node), MPI, job arrays with per-task input mapping, or a minimal template for quick debugging. Which would you like?

results.prompt: How do I write a good Slurm batch script?
results.agent_response:
Good question — a clear, portable Slurm batch script saves time, avoids wasted resources, and makes debugging much easier. Below are concise best practices, common directives, and a practical example you can adapt.

Key principles
- Request only the resources you need (CPUs, GPUs, memory, time). Overestimating wastes scheduler capacity and increases queue delay.
- Make the script self-contained and reproducible: load modules, set env vars, stage data, and log useful output.
- Fail fast and capture failures: use shell safety flags and traps to record exit status and cleanup.
- Test interactively first with a small allocation, then submit the full batch.
- Prefer srun to start parallel/mpi tasks inside the allocation (or use your MPI launcher if required by your MPI stack).

Common SBATCH directives to include
- Job identity and output: --job-name=, --output=, --error= (use %j for jobid and %x for jobname)
- Resources: --partition=, --nodes=, --ntasks=, --cpus-per-task=, --mem=, --gres=gpu:1
- Time and QoS: --time=, --qos=, --account=
- Arrays & dependencies: --array=0-99, --dependency=afterok:<jobid>
- Notifications: --mail-type=END,FAIL --mail-user=you@example.com
- Optional: --exclusive, --constraint=, --hint=nomultithread

Shell-level hygiene
- Start script with a shebang and strict mode:
  set -euo pipefail
- Use trap to record failures and clean temp files:
  trap 'rc=$?; echo "Exiting with $rc"; exit $rc' EXIT
- Use a dedicated working directory (e.g., $SLURM_TMPDIR or a job-specific dir under $SCRATCH)
- Avoid hard-coded absolute paths; use variables and document assumptions.

I/O and staging
- Stage large input data to local disk (NVMe or $TMPDIR) if the job is I/O-heavy; copy results back to persistent storage at end.
- Redirect or compress logs; don’t produce extremely large stdout from many tasks.
- Use checkpointing or periodic saves for long runs.

Parallelism / MPI / GPUs
- Use srun to launch tasks within the allocation: srun --mpi=pmix ./my_mpi_app
- For multi-GPU jobs, request appropriate gres and set CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES if necessary (many clusters set this automatically).
- Set threads/affinity via OMP_NUM_THREADS and --cpus-per-task. Match threads to cores to avoid oversubscription.

Monitoring and post-run reporting
- Add resource reporting: seff $SLURM_JOBID or check sacct/sstat after run.
- Save lightweight runtime logs (elapsed time, memory) for profiling.

Portability & reproducibility
- Record environment: module list; conda env export or pip freeze.
- Consider containers (Singularity/Apptainer) for consistent envs: singularity exec image.sif python train.py

Example batch script
#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --job-name=myjob
#SBATCH --output=logs/%x-%j.out
#SBATCH --error=logs/%x-%j.err
#SBATCH --partition=gpu
#SBATCH --nodes=1
#SBATCH --ntasks=1
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=8
#SBATCH --gres=gpu:1
#SBATCH --mem=32G
#SBATCH --time=04:00:00
#SBATCH --mail-type=END,FAIL
#SBATCH --mail-user=you@example.com
#SBATCH --array=0-9

set -euo pipefail
trap 'rc=$?; echo "Job ${SLURM_JOB_ID} exiting with $rc"; exit $rc' EXIT

echo "Job $SLURM_JOB_ID on $(hostname) started at $(date)"
module purge
module load cuda/11.8 python/3.10
# export OMP_NUM_THREADS to match cpus-per-task
export OMP_NUM_THREADS=${SLURM_CPUS_PER_TASK:-8}

# Optional: copy data to local fast storage
mkdir -p $SLURM_TMPDIR/work
cp -r /scratch/$USER/dataset $SLURM_TMPDIR/work/
cd $SLURM_TMPDIR/work

# Run — use srun so Slurm manages task placement
srun --cpu_bind=cores python train.py --seed ${SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID}

# Copy results back
rsync -av results /scratch/$USER/job-results/${SLURM_JOB_ID}/
echo "Job $SLURM_JOB_ID finished at $(date)"

Quick testing workflow
1) Run interactively: salloc --nodes=1 --gres=gpu:1 --time=00:30:00 --cpus-per-task=4
2) Inside allocation run a small job/script to validate environment and dependencies.
3) Submit with sbatch only after successful interactive test.

Further tips
- Use --gres-flags=enforce-binding or node-specific constraints if GPU binding matters.
- For arrays, keep per-task outputs separate (use %a in filenames).
- Document expected runtime and memory so future runs are easier to size.
- If jobs often fail due to transient cluster issues, add retry logic using dependencies (submit job B with --dependency=afternotok:<A> to retry).

If you want, I can:
- Review a specific script you have and point out improvements (paste it here).
- Generate a template for a common workflow (training, MPI, data preprocessing).

results.prompt: Slurm tutorial
results.agent_response:
Nice — here’s a compact, practical Slurm tutorial you can use as a quick reference or to teach others. It covers the common commands, typical options, examples, monitoring/diagnosis, and best practices.

1) Quick overview
- Slurm manages jobs and resources on an HPC cluster. Common roles:
  - sbatch: submit a batch script (non-interactive)
  - srun: run a task (inside an allocation or from sbatch)
  - salloc: request an interactive allocation
  - squeue / sinfo: view queue and cluster state
  - sacct: historical/accounting info for finished jobs
  - scontrol: inspect or (admin) change detailed records
  - scancel: cancel jobs

2) Basic batch script (sbatch)
- Put scheduler directives at the top with #SBATCH lines. Example:
  #!/bin/bash
  #SBATCH --job-name=myjob
  #SBATCH --partition=gpu
  #SBATCH --nodes=1
  #SBATCH --ntasks=1
  #SBATCH --cpus-per-task=4
  #SBATCH --gres=gpu:1
  #SBATCH --mem=16G
  #SBATCH --time=02:00:00
  #SBATCH --output=job-%j.out

  module load python
  srun python train.py

- Submit with: sbatch myscript.sh
- Output file: slurm-<jobid>.out or whatever you set with --output

3) Interactive work: salloc / srun
- Request interactive allocation:
  salloc --nodes=1 --ntasks=1 --cpus-per-task=4 --gres=gpu:1 --time=01:00:00
  srun --pty bash    # get a shell on allocated node(s)
- Useful for debugging or running interactive sessions.

4) Job arrays and dependencies
- Job arrays (many similar tasks):
  #SBATCH --array=1-100%10
  # inside script use $SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID
- Dependencies (run when another job succeeds):
  sbatch --dependency=afterok:<jobid> next_step.sh
  Common dependency types: afterok, afterany, aftercorr, singleton, expand

5) Common resource options (examples)
- --partition=PARTITION
- --nodes=N
- --ntasks=T  (total MPI tasks)
- --cpus-per-task=C (threads per task)
- --mem=16G  (memory per node by default; some clusters support --mem-per-cpu)
- --gres=gpu:1 (generic consumable resources, e.g., gpu)
- --time=HH:MM:SS
- --job-name=NAME, --output=FILE, --error=FILE
- --account=ACCOUNT, --qos=QOS

6) Monitoring jobs and nodes
- squeue -u $USER  # see your pending/running jobs
- squeue -j <jobid> # job-specific queue row (shows state and REASON column when pending)
- sinfo             # partitions and node counts (allocated/idle/down)
- sinfo -N          # one row per node
- sstat -j <jobid>  # live stats for a running job (CPU/mem/I/O)
- sacct -j <jobid>  # historical accounting for completed jobs (ExitCode, Elapsed, resources)
- scontrol show job <jobid>  # detailed job record (useful for pending Reason=)

7) Diagnosing pending jobs
- First check squeue -j <jobid> (REASON column). Common reasons:
  - Resources / ReqNodeNotAvail: requested nodes/GPUs not free
  - Dependency: waiting on other job(s)
  - Priority / Backfill: lower priority than others
  - BeginTime: job has a start time in the future
  - AssocGrp / AssocMax: account or resource limits reached
- If squeue’s reason is blank or terse, use: scontrol show job <jobid> to see Reason=... and more details.
- If job is missing from squeue, use sacct -j <jobid> to see whether it already completed/failed.

8) Inspecting node and partition health
- sinfo shows partition-level free/alloc/down counts.
- sinfo -R or sinfo_reasons (admin) shows nodes listed with reasons (drain/down reasons).
- scontrol show node <nodename> gives detailed node attributes.

9) Logs, outputs, and debugging
- Standard output written to --output file (or slurm-<jobid>.out by default).
- For crashes, check ExitCode in sacct or the slurm output file and any application logs.
- Use small test jobs first (short time, small resources) to ensure environment/modules and scripts behave correctly.

10) Accounting, priority, and history
- sacct for historical records (states, exit codes, elapsed).
- sreport for usage reports (CPU/GPU-hours).
- sshare for fairshare information; sprio shows per-job priority factors.
- scontrol_license lists licenses tracked by Slurm.

11) Useful admin/diagnostic commands (read-only)
- sdiag   # scheduler diagnostics (backfill efficiency, cycle times)
- sprio   # job priority listing
- scontrol show config  # controller configuration values
- scontrol ping  # check controller responsiveness

12) Best practices
- Request realistic resources (don’t over-request CPUs/GPU/time).
- Always set a time limit (--time). Over-long requests can delay scheduling and waste quota.
- Use job arrays for parameter sweeps instead of many independent submissions.
- Name jobs and route logs to per-job files (--job-name and --output).
- Test interactively or with tiny jobs before large runs.
- Check pending reason before increasing resources — sometimes the job is blocked by account/QOS limits, not lack of nodes.
- Use modules/environment to keep reproducible environments. Consider container solutions if supported.

13) Examples (quick)
- Submit a simple CPU job:
  sbatch --job-name=test --time=00:10:00 --cpus-per-task=2 --mem=4G myscript.sh
- Submit a GPU job:
  sbatch --partition=gpu --gres=gpu:1 --time=04:00:00 gpu_script.sh
- Cancel a job:
  scancel <jobid>   (operator/admin command — cancels the job)
- Check why job is pending:
  squeue -j <jobid>   then scontrol show job <jobid>

14) Where to learn more
- Man pages: man sbatch, man srun, man squeue
- Slurm docs: https://slurm.schedmd.com/ (includes job reason codes, sbatch examples, configuration)
- If you want, tell me what you’re trying to run (resources, partition, GPU/CPU, time), and I’ll draft an sbatch script or help debug a pending job.

results.prompt: Show me a safe sbatch script pattern
results.agent_response:
Below is a compact, production‑safe sbatch script pattern with explanations of the important safety / reproducibility practices. Copy and adapt the resource lines to your cluster's partitions and policies.

#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --job-name=myjob                  # short, descriptive name
#SBATCH --output=logs/%x-%j.out           # %x=job name, %j=jobid
#SBATCH --error=logs/%x-%j.err
#SBATCH --time=02:00:00                   # wall time limit (HH:MM:SS)
#SBATCH --partition=gpu                   # change to your partition
#SBATCH --nodes=1
#SBATCH --ntasks=1
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=8
#SBATCH --mem=32G
#SBATCH --gres=gpu:1                      # only if you need GPUs
#SBATCH --mail-type=END,FAIL
#SBATCH --mail-user=you@example.com
#SBATCH --chdir=$HOME/myproject           # run from project dir
#SBATCH --export=NONE                     # start with a clean env; export what you need

set -euo pipefail
umask 002

# Prepare local (ephemeral) working dir and ensure logs exist
mkdir -p logs
SCRATCH=${SLURM_TMPDIR:-/tmp/$USER/job-$SLURM_JOB_ID}
mkdir -p "$SCRATCH"

# Cleanup / copy-back on exit or signal (best-effort)
finish() {
  rc=$?
  echo "[$(date -Is)] Job $SLURM_JOB_ID exiting with code $rc"
  mkdir -p "$HOME/job-results/$SLURM_JOB_ID"
  rsync -a --remove-source-files "$SCRATCH"/ "$HOME/job-results/$SLURM_JOB_ID/" || true
  exit $rc
}
trap finish EXIT INT TERM

# Load only required modules and set parallelism env vars explicitly
module purge
module load python/3.10
module load cuda/11.8                     # if using GPUs

export OMP_NUM_THREADS=${OMP_NUM_THREADS:-$SLURM_CPUS_PER_TASK}
export MKL_NUM_THREADS=${MKL_NUM_THREADS:-$OMP_NUM_THREADS}

# Report what Slurm gave you (useful for debugging)
echo "JOB: $SLURM_JOB_ID ($SLURM_JOB_NAME)"
echo "Nodes: $SLURM_JOB_NODELIST"
echo "CPUS_PER_TASK: $SLURM_CPUS_PER_TASK  NTASKS: $SLURM_NTASKS"
echo "TMPDIR: $SCRATCH"

# Use srun for the actual workload; it takes care of task launch & resource binding
srun --cpu_bind=cores ./run_my_workload.sh --output-dir "$SCRATCH"

Key safety & best-practices explained
- set -euo pipefail + trap: fail early on errors, and run a cleanup/copy-back even on signals (preemption).
- --export=NONE: prevents accidental propagation of your local environment; explicitly export variables you need.
- Use SLURM-provided env vars (SLURM_CPUS_PER_TASK, SLURM_JOB_NODELIST, SLURM_TMPDIR) rather than guessing resource layout.
- Run from a project directory (via --chdir) and use $SLURM_TMPDIR for scratch I/O to avoid NFS bottlenecks.
- Use module purge/load so predictable software versions are used.
- Use srun to launch tasks (not plain exec), and prefer srun --cpu_bind/-–mpi flags for correct binding.
- For GPU jobs: request --gres=gpu:N; Slurm typically sets CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES for you — do not hardcode device ids.
- Small test runs: before a long/large job, test the script with a short --time and minimal resources.
- Logging: send output to per-job files (include jobid), and keep job-specific persistent copies (rsync back on exit).
- Avoid destructive commands and avoid running as root. Limit writes to your project and $SLURM_TMPDIR.

## EXAMPLES[#SECTION_EXAMPLES](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
Specify a batch script by filename on the command line. The batch script specifies a 1 minute time limit for the job.

```text
$ sbatch -N4 #!/bin/sh > srun hostname |sort > EOF sbatch: Submitted batch job 65541 $ cat slurm-65541.out host1 host2 host3 host4
```
To create a heterogeneous job with 3 components, each allocating a unique set of nodes:
```text
$ sbatch -w node[2-3] : -w node4 : -w node[5-7] work.bash Submitted batch job 34987
```

results.prompt: Explain basic Slurm submission steps
results.agent_response:
Here’s a concise, practical walkthrough of the basic Slurm job submission steps and the common commands/options you’ll use.

1) Create a batch script
- Start with a shell shebang (e.g., #!/bin/bash).
- Add resource and metadata directives with #SBATCH lines (these are read by Slurm, not the shell).
  Typical #SBATCH settings:
  - --job-name=NAME
  - --partition=partition_name
  - --time=HH:MM:SS
  - --nodes=N
  - --ntasks=TOTAL_TASKS
  - --cpus-per-task=CPUS
  - --mem=MEM (e.g., 32G)
  - --gres=gpu:1 (for GPUs)
  - --account=account_name or --qos=...
  - --output=slurm-%j.out and --error=...
- Load modules / set up environment and run commands (use srun for parallel tasks or program launches).

Example minimal script (plain text):
#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --job-name=myjob
#SBATCH --partition=short
#SBATCH --time=01:00:00
#SBATCH --nodes=1
#SBATCH --ntasks=1
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=4
#SBATCH --mem=8G
#SBATCH --output=slurm-%j.out

module load python
srun python train.py --epochs 10

2) Submit the job
- sbatch myscript.sh
  - sbatch prints the assigned job ID and exits (job may be pending).

3) Monitor the job
- squeue -u yourusername (or squeue -j <jobid>) to see RUNNING/PENDING state and pending reason.
- sstat -j <jobid> (for live running job resource stats).
- tail -f slurm-<jobid>.out to watch program output (when it’s produced).

4) Post-run / accounting
- sacct -j <jobid> (or sacct -u username) to see final state, exit code, elapsed time, resources used.
- Output files: slurm-<jobid>.out (by default, or as set via --output).

5) Cancel or change jobs
- scancel <jobid> to cancel.
- Use scontrol show job <jobid> for detailed job configuration/status (admin details).
- You can update some properties with scontrol (admin or permitted users only).

6) Useful advanced features (brief)
- Job arrays: #SBATCH --array=1-100 to run many similar tasks with one submission (use %A, %a, %j in filenames).
- Dependencies: sbatch --dependency=afterok:<jobid> to chain jobs.
- Interactive allocations: salloc (request resources interactively) or srun --pty bash.
- GPUs: request with --gres=gpu:N and ensure you pick the correct partition/QOS that allows GPUs.
- Environment vars available in job: SLURM_JOB_ID, SLURM_NTASKS, SLURM_CPUS_PER_TASK, etc.

7) Common pitfalls/tips
- Always request sufficient time; jobs killed for exceeding the time limit are lost.
- Choose the correct partition/QOS and account to avoid priority/accounting issues.
- Put module loads and path setup in the script; the batch environment is non-interactive.
- Direct output to identifiable files (use %j token for jobid).
- For multi-process MPI or task-parallel workloads, use srun (not plain exec) so Slurm launches tasks correctly.

If you want, I can:
- Review a script you have and point out problems, or
- Show an example sbatch for a GPU training job or an MPI job. Which would you prefer?

results.prompt: Show me a safe sbatch script pattern
results.agent_response:
Below is a compact, safe sbatch script pattern with comments and best-practices you can adapt. It focuses on shell safety, reproducible environment, sensible SLURM directives, proper use of srun, temporary-scratch handling, logging, and cleanup/checkpoint hooks.

#!/usr/bin/env bash
#SBATCH --job-name=myjob                # short, human-friendly job name
#SBATCH --output=%x-%j.out              # %x = job name, %j = jobid
#SBATCH --error=%x-%j.err
#SBATCH --partition=gpu                  # change to your partition
#SBATCH --nodes=1
#SBATCH --ntasks=1
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=8
#SBATCH --mem=32G
#SBATCH --gres=gpu:1                     # request GPUs only if needed
#SBATCH --time=02:00:00
#SBATCH --mail-type=END,FAIL
#SBATCH --mail-user=you@example.com
#SBATCH --chdir=/home/you/workdir        # optional: ensure working dir exists
#SBATCH --export=NONE                    # safer than ALL; export only what you need

# ---- Shell safety ----
set -euo pipefail
IFS=$'\n\t'
umask 0022

# ---- Job metadata ----
echo "Job $SLURM_JOB_ID ($SLURM_JOB_NAME) starting on $(hostname) at $(date)"
echo "Nodes: $SLURM_JOB_NODELIST; NTASKS=$SLURM_NTASKS; CPUS_PER_TASK=$SLURM_CPUS_PER_TASK"

# ---- Prepare a per-job scratch dir (use $TMPDIR if available) ----
export SCRATCH_DIR="${TMPDIR:-/tmp/$USER/job-$SLURM_JOB_ID}"
mkdir -p "$SCRATCH_DIR"
echo "Scratch: $SCRATCH_DIR"

# ---- Cleanup/rsync-on-exit and trap ----
cleanup() {
  rc=$?
  echo "Job exiting with code $rc at $(date)"
  # copy results back (adjust destination)
  rsync -av --remove-source-files "$SCRATCH_DIR/" /home/you/results/"$SLURM_JOB_ID"/ || echo "rsync failed"
  rm -rf "$SCRATCH_DIR"
  exit $rc
}
trap cleanup EXIT

# ---- Environment modules / conda / venv ----
module purge
module load python/3.10 cuda/11.8   # change to what your cluster provides
# source /path/to/venv/bin/activate   # or conda activate, if available

# Export only safe/needed variables (avoid exporting secrets)
export PATH=/home/you/opt/bin:$PATH
export OMP_NUM_THREADS=${SLURM_CPUS_PER_TASK:-8}

# ---- Run with srun (not plain backgrounding) ----
# Use srun so Slurm tracks process tree, accounting, and signals correctly.
srun --cpu_bind=cores python train.py \
  --data /home/you/data \
  --out "$SCRATCH_DIR"/output \
  --epochs 10

# ---- Optional explicit checkpoint before exit ----
# cp "$SCRATCH_DIR"/output/checkpoint.pt /home/you/results/"$SLURM_JOB_ID"/

Notes / best-practices (short):
- Use #SBATCH directives (top of file) not inline shell variables; sbatch reads them before execution.
- set -euo pipefail + IFS prevents subtle script failures and accidental use of unset vars.
- Prefer --export=NONE and then explicitly export only safe vars (avoid leaking API keys).
- Always launch workload with srun (or mpirun integrated with srun) so Slurm manages tasks and signals.
- Use %j (jobid) and/or %x (job name) in output/error filenames to avoid collisions.
- Use TMPDIR or a per-job scratch area; stage input files in, write outputs there, then rsync back in trap.
- Trap EXIT and also handle SIGTERM/SIGINT for orderly cleanup and checkpointing.
- Test interactively with salloc or small resources/time before a full run.
- For job arrays, use: #SBATCH --array=0-9%4 and access SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID in the script.
- If requesting GPUs, assume exclusive allocation; do not set CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES manually unless your cluster requires it (Slurm often sets CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES).
- Keep memory/cpu/gpu requests accurate to avoid unexpected OOMs and scheduling delays.

If you want, I can:
- produce a variant for MPI (multi-node) or a GPU deep-learning template,
- show a minimal job-array example,
- or adapt this template for conda activation and checkpointing specifics. Which one would you like?

results.prompt: Explain basic Slurm submission steps
results.agent_response:
Below is a concise, practical overview of the basic steps to submit and manage a Slurm batch job, with small examples and common tips.

1) Create a batch script
- A batch script is a shell script that contains resource directives in lines beginning with #SBATCH (these are parsed by Slurm).
- Common #SBATCH options:
  - --job-name=NAME
  - --output=FILE (defaults to slurm-%j.out)
  - --error=FILE
  - --partition=PARTITION
  - --nodes=N
  - --ntasks=N
  - --cpus-per-task=N
  - --mem=16G or --mem-per-cpu=4G
  - --time=HH:MM:SS
  - --gres=gpu:1 (for GPUs)
  - --account=ACCOUNT and --qos=QOS
  - --array=1-100%10 (job arrays)
- Example minimal script (myscript.sh):
  #!/bin/bash
  #SBATCH --job-name=myjob
  #SBATCH --output=job-%j.out
  #SBATCH --partition=gpu
  #SBATCH --nodes=1
  #SBATCH --ntasks=1
  #SBATCH --cpus-per-task=4
  #SBATCH --mem=16G
  #SBATCH --time=02:00:00
  #SBATCH --gres=gpu:1

  module load python
  srun python train.py

Notes:
- #SBATCH directives must appear before the first non-comment, non-whitespace line.
- Slurm sets environment variables you can use in the script (SLURM_JOB_ID, SLURM_NTASKS, SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID, etc.).

2) Submit the job
- Submit with: sbatch myscript.sh
- sbatch prints the new job ID (e.g., "Submitted batch job 12345").

3) Monitor the job
- View queued/running jobs: squeue or squeue -u $USER
- View a specific job: squeue -j <jobid>
- For why a job is pending, squeue shows the REASON column; for more detail: scontrol show job <jobid>
- For runtime stats of a RUNNING job: sstat -j <jobid>
- For completed/failed history: sacct -j <jobid>

4) Interactive allocations (if you need a shell)
- Request an interactive allocation: salloc --ntasks=1 --time=01:00:00
- Then run an interactive command/shell: srun --pty bash

5) Job control
- Cancel a job: scancel <jobid>
- Hold/release: scontrol hold <jobid> / scontrol release <jobid> (admin or allowed users)
- Requeue: scontrol requeue <jobid>
- Use dependencies: sbatch --dependency=afterok:<jobid> nextscript.sh

6) Job arrays
- Submit arrays with --array=START-END[%MAX_CONCURRENT]
- Use $SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID inside the script to distinguish tasks.

7) Common troubleshooting tips
- If pending, check REASON from squeue and scontrol show job <jobid> — reasons include resources, priority, QOS/account limits, reservation, or partition down.
- Ensure you requested the right partition, account, and walltime. Underestimating time can cause premature TIMEOUT.
- For MPI and multi-node jobs, prefer srun to launch MPI ranks (or follow site-specific MPI instructions).
- Check output files (default slurm-%j.out) for job stdout/stderr.
- If GPU requested, use --gres=gpu:<count> and ensure your job uses the GPUs (CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES is typically set for you).

8) Useful commands summary
- sbatch myscript.sh — submit
- squeue [-u $USER] — view queue
- scontrol show job <jobid> — detailed job info
- sstat -j <jobid> — runtime stats (running jobs)
- sacct -j <jobid> — historical accounting
- scancel <jobid> — cancel

If you want, I can:
- Review a sample script you have and suggest fixes/optimizations.
- Show an example for a GPU/MPP/array job tailored to your workload. Which would you like?
