results.prompt: Slurm tutorial
results.agent_response:
Good — here’s a concise, practical Slurm tutorial you can use as a quick reference and to get started writing and running jobs.

Core concepts
- Controller and daemons: slurmctld schedules; slurmd runs on compute nodes.
- Job vs step: an sbatch/salloc job can contain multiple srun steps.
- Partitions: named pools of nodes (like "gpu", "cpu", "debug").
- Resources: nodes, CPUs (tasks/CPUs-per-task), memory, GPUs (gres), time limit, QOS, account.

Common commands (read-only vs actions)
- sbatch <script.sh> — submit a batch job (non-interactive).
- srun [options] <command> — run a job step; used inside allocations or for interactive runs.
- salloc [options] — get an interactive allocation; then use srun inside it.
- squeue — view queued/running jobs (use -u USER, -p PARTITION, -j JOBID).
- sinfo — view partitions and node states (allocated/idle/down).
- scontrol show job <JOBID> — detailed job info and scheduling reasons.
- sacct — accounting/history for completed jobs.
- sstat -j <JOBID> — runtime stats for running jobs (CPU/memory I/O).
- scancel <JOBID|--user=> — cancel jobs.
- scontrol (node/calendar/reservation commands) — admin operations.

Simple batch job example (sbatch)
Example job script (save as train.sh):
#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --job-name=train-model
#SBATCH --output=train-%j.out
#SBATCH --error=train-%j.err
#SBATCH --partition=gpu
#SBATCH --nodes=1
#SBATCH --ntasks=1
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=8
#SBATCH --gres=gpu:1
#SBATCH --mem=32G
#SBATCH --time=02:00:00

module load cuda/12.1 python/3.10
echo "Job $SLURM_JOB_ID on $SLURM_JOB_NODELIST"
srun python train.py --epochs 10

Notes:
- %j in output is job ID. Use module/environment setup as your cluster requires.
- Request realistic walltime; jobs killed when time limit reached.

Interactive usage
- salloc --nodes=1 --ntasks=1 --gres=gpu:1 --time=01:00:00
  After allocation runs, use srun --pty bash to get an interactive shell on compute node.
- Or srun --pty --nodes=1 --gres=gpu:1 bash for a direct interactive step (may be limited on some clusters).

Job arrays
- sbatch --array=1-100%10 my-array.sh
- Inside the script use $SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID to index inputs.
- %10 limits concurrency to 10 array tasks at once.

Dependencies
- sbatch --dependency=afterok:12345 myjob.sh  (run only if job 12345 succeeded)
- Other types: after, afterany, aftercorr, singleton, expand.

Monitoring and diagnosing
- squeue -u $USER or squeue -j <JOBID> -o "%i %P %j %u %T %M %D %R"
  Columns: JOBID PARTITION NAME USER STATE TIME NODES NODELIST(REASON)
- If a job is PENDING, look at the REASON column (e.g., Resources, QOSMaxCpuLimit, Dependency, PartitionDown).
- If squeue’s reason is empty/unhelpful, run scontrol show job <JOBID> for detailed reason and constraints.
- sinfo -s or sinfo -N shows partition summary and node states (ALLOCATED/IDLE/DOWN); check where resources are available.
- For recent finished jobs use sacct -u username -S starttime to see exit codes and elapsed times.

Common pending reasons and how to act
- Resources: no suitable nodes/GPUs match your request; try smaller/other partition, relax constraints, or wait.
- QOS/QOSMaxCpuLimit: you hit QOS/account limits — ask admin or change QOS/account.
- Priority: job is low priority; sprio shows priority factors.
- PartitionDown/NodeDown: the partition or nodes are unavailable — check sinfo and contact admin.
- Dependency: job waiting for dependent job to finish; verify dependency is correct.

Best practices
- Test on small resources and short time first.
- Request only the CPUs/GPU/memory/time you need — oversized requests increase queue wait.
- Use job arrays for many similar tasks rather than separate sbatch calls.
- Use --output and --error files (with %j) to capture logs.
- Rely on sacct for post-mortem (ExitCode shows why a job failed or was killed).
- Don’t run heavy I/O or long experiments on login nodes.
- Use modules or container images (Singularity/Apptainer) for reproducible environments.
- Consider checkpointing for long runs so you can restart after node preemption.

Useful advanced tools
- scontrol show config — controller configuration (admin).
- sdiag / sprio — scheduler diagnostics and job priorities.
- sreport — usage reports (CPU/GPU-hours by user/account).
- scontrol show reservation — reservation info.
- scontrol license — license usage tracked by Slurm.

Quick troubleshooting workflow for a stuck PENDING job
1) squeue -j JOBID -o "%i %P %j %u %T %M %D %R" — note reason.
2) If REASON is ambiguous, scontrol show job JOBID — look for ReqNodeList, TRES, Partition, Depend.
3) sinfo -l or sinfo -N to check whether nodes/partitions that match your constraints are idle.
4) If limits (QOS/account) suspected, check with your admin or sacctmgr queries.
5) If running but slow/unexpected errors, use sstat -j JOBID and inspect output files.

Where to read more
- Official Slurm docs: https://slurm.schedmd.com (look up sbatch, srun, squeue, sinfo, sacct, scontrol).
- Your cluster’s README or runbook (local policies, partitions, module names, accounts).

If you want, I can:
- Review a job script you’re about to submit.
- Create an sbatch template tuned for a GPU job (tell me requested GPUs, CPUs, memory, time, partition).
- Inspect the live queue or nodes on your cluster (I can run squeue/sinfo — tell me which).

results.prompt: Show me a safe sbatch script pattern
results.agent_response:
Below is a compact, practical, “safe” sbatch script pattern you can copy and adapt. It focuses on bash safety (fail fast, predictable IFS/umask), Slurm best-practices (explicit resource requests, clear output names), signal handling and cleanup (trap), using node-local temporary storage, and simple guards (validate inputs, don't assume allocations). After the template are brief notes explaining the important parts.

Example: safe single-job sbatch template
#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --job-name=safe_job                # job name
#SBATCH --output=%x-%j.out                 # %x = job name, %j = jobid
#SBATCH --error=%x-%j.err
#SBATCH --mail-type=END,FAIL
#SBATCH --mail-user=you@example.com
#SBATCH --time=01:00:00
#SBATCH --partition=short
#SBATCH --ntasks=1
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=4
#SBATCH --mem=8G
# Uncomment if you need GPUs:
# SBATCH --gres=gpu:1
#SBATCH --chdir=/home/$USER/workdir      # run from submit dir (or set explicitly)

# Bash safety
set -euo pipefail
IFS=$'\n\t'
umask 0022

# Basic environment checks
: "${SLURM_JOB_ID:?SLURM_JOB_ID missing — run under Slurm?}"
SUBMIT_DIR="${SLURM_SUBMIT_DIR:-$PWD}"
echo "Starting job $SLURM_JOB_ID ($SLURM_JOB_NAME) on $(hostname) at $(date)"
echo "Submit dir: $SUBMIT_DIR"

# Create a node-local temporary workspace (avoid NFS for heavy IO)
TMPDIR="${TMPDIR:-/tmp}/${USER}_${SLURM_JOB_ID}"
mkdir -p "$TMPDIR"
trap 'rc=$?; echo "Exit trap: rc=$rc; cleaning $TMPDIR"; rm -rf "$TMPDIR"; exit $rc' EXIT

# Optional: attempt to requeue if preempted (may require permission)
on_term() {
  echo "Received SIGTERM at $(date). Attempting to requeue job $SLURM_JOB_ID"
  if command -v scontrol >/dev/null 2>&1; then
    scontrol requeue "$SLURM_JOB_ID" || echo "Requeue failed or not permitted"
  fi
  exit 1
}
trap 'on_term' TERM

# Load modules / activate environment
module purge
module load python/3.10 cuda/12.0    # adapt to your site modules or use conda/venv

# Validate inputs (fail early)
INPUT_FILE="$SUBMIT_DIR/input.dat"
if [[ ! -r "$INPUT_FILE" ]]; then
  echo "ERROR: input file not found or unreadable: $INPUT_FILE" >&2
  exit 2
fi

# Respect allocated resources: example check for GPUs
if [[ -n "${SLURM_JOB_GPUS:-}" || -n "${CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES:-}" ]]; then
  echo "GPUs visible: ${CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES:-$SLURM_JOB_GPUS}"
fi

# Main work: run under srun for proper accounting / resource binding
srun --cpu_bind=cores --pty my_program --input "$INPUT_FILE" --outdir "$TMPDIR" \
  2>&1 | tee "$SUBMIT_DIR/${SLURM_JOB_NAME}-${SLURM_JOB_ID}.log"

# Copy results back reliably
rsync -a --chmod=ugo=rwX "$TMPDIR"/ "$SUBMIT_DIR"/results/ || echo "Warning: rsync failed"

echo "Job $SLURM_JOB_ID finished at $(date)"

Short checklist / rationale (quick)
- set -euo pipefail + IFS: makes failures immediate and predictable.
- umask: ensure output files have sane permissions.
- Explicit SBATCH resource requests: required to avoid oversubscription and to make the scheduler happy.
- --output/--error with %x/%j: makes logs easy to match to jobs.
- Use node-local TMPDIR for heavy IO and rsync results back to submit dir at the end — reduces NFS contention.
- Trap EXIT and TERM: ensure cleanup; attempt requeue on TERM (note: may need permission).
- Use srun for the main command: ensures Slurm applies CPU/GPU binding and accounting correctly.
- Validate inputs early and fail with clear messages.
- Avoid embedding secrets in scripts; read credentials from secure stores if required.
- Limit privileges: run as normal user, not root. Avoid sudo inside batch jobs unless expressly permitted.

Variations / extras
- Array jobs: use SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID and create per-task TMPDIR subdirectories.
- Checkpointing: write periodic checkpoints to node-local disk and rsync to persistent storage in trap/regular intervals.
- Resource guards: check SLURM_CPUS_ON_NODE / SLURM_GPUS to adapt thread counts (e.g., OMP_NUM_THREADS).
- For GPU jobs, set CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES from SLURM to avoid contention (your cluster may already set this).

If you want, I can:
- produce a GPU-array version that sets CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES and per-task TMP directories, or
- tailor the template to your workflow (Python training, MPI, checkpointing frequency, or site-specific module names). Which would you prefer?

results.prompt: Slurm tutorial
results.agent_response:
Nice — here’s a compact, practical Slurm tutorial covering the commands, job script basics, common options, monitoring, debugging, and best practices.

Core commands (what you’ll use most)
- sbatch <script> — submit a batch job (non-interactive).
- srun [...] — launch tasks inside an allocation (also used for interactive shells).
- salloc [...] — get an allocation interactively (useful for debugging or interactive runs).
- squeue — show the job queue (status, pending reasons).
- sinfo — show partitions and node states (idle/alloc/down counts).
- scancel <jobid> — cancel a job.
- scontrol show job <jobid> — show detailed job info (reasons, resources).
- sacct — accounting/history for completed jobs.
- sstat -j <jobid> — runtime stats for running jobs.
- scontrol show config / lookup_slurm_docs — cluster/scheduler configuration and docs.

Minimal sbatch script template
- Save as run.sh (make executable optional). Submit with: sbatch run.sh
Example script (plain text):
#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --job-name=myjob
#SBATCH --output=slurm-%j.out
#SBATCH --error=slurm-%j.err
#SBATCH --time=01:00:00          # HH:MM:SS
#SBATCH --nodes=1
#SBATCH --ntasks=1
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=4
#SBATCH --mem=16G
#SBATCH --partition=standard
#SBATCH --gres=gpu:1             # request GPUs when available
# module load python/3.10
srun python train.py --epochs 10

Important SBATCH options
- --time= (wallclock limit)
- --nodes=, --ntasks= (MPI/tasks)
- --cpus-per-task= (threads per task, e.g., OpenMP)
- --mem= or --mem-per-cpu=
- --partition= (queue/partition name)
- --gres=gpu:<n> (GPU request)
- --job-name=, --output=, --error=
- --account= and --qos= (accounting and priority)
- --mail-user=, --mail-type=BEGIN,END,FAIL
- --array=1-100%10 (job arrays)
- --dependency=afterok:<jobid> (chaining jobs)

Job arrays and environment variables
- #SBATCH --array=1-100%10 creates many similar tasks limited to 10 concurrent.
- Use $SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID inside the script to index work.
Useful env vars inside jobs:
- SLURM_JOB_ID, SLURM_JOB_NODELIST, SLURM_NTASKS, SLURM_CPUS_PER_TASK, SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID, SLURM_SUBMIT_DIR

Interactive debugging and short tests
- srun --pty --partition=debug --time=00:30:00 --gres=gpu:1 bash
- salloc -N1 -n1 --time=00:30:00  (gives an interactive allocation)
Use small resources/time to iterate quickly before large runs.

Monitoring and diagnosing jobs
- squeue -u $USER  (your jobs)
- squeue -j <jobid> -o "%i %P %j %u %T %M %R"  (custom columns; %R shows reason)
- If a job is PENDING, squeue usually shows a short reason; for more detail:
  scontrol show job <jobid>
- Check node/partition status with sinfo (sinfo -s or sinfo -Nel for node list)
- For running job stats: sstat -j <jobid>
- After a job finishes, use sacct -j <jobid> --format=JobID,JobName,State,ExitCode,Elapsed,AllocCPUS,MaxRSS

Common reasons a job won’t start
- No eligible nodes in the requested partition (use sinfo to inspect nodes).
- You exceeded account/QOS limits or per-user limits.
- Waiting for resources from another job (priority/priority factors).
- Node feature/GPU counts not available (gres mismatch).
- Partition is down or drained.

Failure/debugging checklist
- Inspect slurm-<jobid>.out and .err files.
- Use scontrol show job <jobid> for reason and resource requests.
- Use sacct to see ExitCode and whether it timed out.
- Test interactively (srun/salloc) with the same command.
- Check modules, conda/env activation, and paths — often missing environment is root cause.
- Ensure requested memory/CPUs match the program’s needs (OOM kills if too small).

Performance & best practices
- Right-size resources (ask for what you need, not a lot more).
- Use cpus-per-task for threaded apps and ntasks for MPI processes.
- Use job arrays for many parallel short tasks.
- Use checkpointing for long jobs (so you can resume).
- Stage data locally on the compute node if I/O is a bottleneck.
- Start with short, small jobs to validate scripts before full runs.

Advanced features (quick pointers)
- job dependencies: sbatch --dependency=afterok:123 job2.sh
- heterogeneous jobs: sbatch with multiple -w or heterogeneous resource spec
- reservations: admins can create named reservations (scontrol show reservation ...)
- fairshare/priority view: sprio or sshare
- licenses: scontrol_license shows license usage

Where to read more
- man sbatch, srun, squeue, sinfo, sacct, scontrol
- Official Slurm docs: https://slurm.schedmd.com/
- If you want, I can fetch command reference snippets or create a custom example for your workflow (MPI, TensorFlow/PyTorch GPU training, Slurm arrays, or debugging). What would you like next?

results.prompt: How do I write a good Slurm batch script?
results.agent_response:
Good question — a “good” sbatch script is clear, minimal, reproducible, and requests exactly the resources your job needs. Below are concise best practices, a short checklist, and a few practical templates you can copy/modify.

Key principles
- Put all #SBATCH directives at the top of the file (they are only parsed until the first non-comment, non-whitespace line).
- #SBATCH lines are read literally (no shell expansion). If you need shell variables, set them after the directives.
- Request precise resources (CPUs, memory, GPUs, time). Over-requesting wastes queue priority; under-requesting causes failures.
- Use srun to launch tasks inside the allocation (srun integrates with Slurm’s task placement and accounting).
- Make scripts reproducible: load modules, set environment, record versions/args, and write output to a known location.
- Test quickly with small resources/time before scaling up to full runs.

Minimal checklist (before you submit)
- Job name (--job-name)
- Partition/account/QoS (--partition, -A, --qos) if required by your site
- Walltime (--time) — keep it conservative for testing
- CPUs and memory (--cpus-per-task, --mem or --mem-per-cpu)
- GPUs if needed (--gres=gpu:1)
- Output and error files (--output, --error), use %j/%x for jobid/name
- Modules, conda/env activation, and environment setup
- Use local scratch ($TMPDIR or /tmp) for heavy I/O and stage results back
- Small test run first (reduced problem size/time)

Useful SBATCH options (common)
- --job-name=NAME
- --output=path/slurm-%j.out and --error=path/slurm-%j.err (or --output with %j)
- --partition=PARTITION
- --time=HH:MM:SS
- --nodes=N, --ntasks=NTASKS, --ntasks-per-node=, --cpus-per-task=CPUS
- --mem=4G or --mem-per-cpu=2G
- --gres=gpu:VENDOR:COUNT or simply --gres=gpu:COUNT
- --mail-type=BEGIN,END,FAIL and --mail-user=you@example.com
- --array=1-100%20  (job arrays; use SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID)
- --exclusive  (if you need exclusive access to nodes)
- --constraint=some-hardware-tag (if needed)

Good script hygiene (inside the script)
- Use a shebang: #!/bin/bash (or /bin/sh, /bin/zsh)
- set -euo pipefail and optionally set -x when debugging
- Load modules explicitly (module purge; module load ...)
- Export any variables your program needs
- Use srun for parallel/MP tasks (srun my_executable) rather than plain ./app
- Use $SLURM_* environment variables for dynamic placement info (SLURM_NTASKS, SLURM_JOB_ID, SLURM_NNODES, SLURM_NODELIST, SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID)
- Stage input to node-local storage, run, then copy results out
- Log environment: date, hostname, module list, git commit or binary version

Templates

1) Simple single-node CPU job
#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --job-name=myjob
#SBATCH --output=logs/%x-%j.out
#SBATCH --error=logs/%x-%j.err
#SBATCH --time=02:00:00
#SBATCH --partition=standard
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=8
#SBATCH --mem=16G

set -euo pipefail
module purge
module load python/3.10
echo "Job $SLURM_JOB_ID started on $(hostname) at $(date)"
srun python my_script.py --input data/input.dat --threads $SLURM_CPUS_PER_TASK

2) GPU job (single GPU)
#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --job-name=gpu-train
#SBATCH --output=logs/%x-%j.out
#SBATCH --time=12:00:00
#SBATCH --partition=gpu
#SBATCH --gres=gpu:1
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=4
#SBATCH --mem=32G

set -euo pipefail
module purge
module load cuda/12.1 cudnn
module load python/3.10
source /path/to/venv/bin/activate
echo "Job $SLURM_JOB_ID on $SLURM_JOB_NODELIST"
srun python train.py --config conf.yaml

3) Job array (embarrassingly parallel tasks)
#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --job-name=array-job
#SBATCH --output=logs/%x-%A_%a.out
#SBATCH --array=1-100%10
#SBATCH --time=00:30:00
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=2
#SBATCH --mem=4G

set -euo pipefail
TASK_ID=$SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID
echo "Array task $TASK_ID on $SLURM_JOB_NODELIST"
srun ./task_runner.sh ${TASK_ID}

4) MPI job (multiple nodes)
#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --job-name=mpi-job
#SBATCH --nodes=4
#SBATCH --ntasks-per-node=16
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=1
#SBATCH --time=04:00:00
#SBATCH --output=logs/%x-%j.out

module purge
module load mpi/openmpi
srun --mpi=pmix ./my_mpi_executable -n ${SLURM_NTASKS}

Debugging tips
- For debugging interactively use salloc or srun --pty bash to get an interactive allocation.
- Use small time and resource requests for first submissions.
- Check slurm output (slurm-<jobid>.out or your --output file) and sacct -j <jobid> for exit codes and CPU/time usage.
- If a job is pending, squeue shows the pending reason; scontrol show job <id> gives more details.

Common mistakes to avoid
- Expecting shell variables to expand in #SBATCH lines (they won’t).
- Forgetting to request enough memory (OOMs kill jobs).
- Not using srun for MPI/parallel launches, which can lead to incorrect placement or missing accounting.
- Writing heavy I/O directly to shared filesystems without staging to local storage.

If you want, tell me:
- whether your job is CPU-only, GPU, MPI, or an array,
- how many nodes/CPUs/GPUs you think you need,
and I’ll write a tailored sbatch script for your workload.

results.prompt: Slurm tutorial
results.agent_response:
Good — here’s a compact, practical Slurm tutorial you can use as a quick reference or cheat‑sheet. Tell me if you want example scripts tuned to your cluster (GPU vs CPU, modules, or particular partitions).

1) Big picture
- Slurm is a job scheduler: users request resources and submit jobs; the controller allocates nodes and runs job steps.
- Common command families:
  - Submit batch jobs: sbatch (non-interactive, runs a script).
  - Run tasks/steps: srun (within an allocation or for interactive runs).
  - Request interactive allocations: salloc (gives you a shell with resources).
  - Query cluster/queue: squeue, sinfo.
  - Detailed info / admin actions: scontrol.
  - Accounting/history: sacct, sreport.
  - Per-job runtime stats: sstat.

2) Typical workflow
- Prepare a job script (shell file with #SBATCH directives).
- Submit with sbatch path/to/script.sh → returns job ID.
- Monitor with squeue, inspect details with scontrol show job <jobid>.
- When finished, inspect output files (stdout/stderr) and/or sacct for accounting info.

3) Minimal job script example
#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --job-name=myjob
#SBATCH --partition=standard
#SBATCH --nodes=1
#SBATCH --ntasks=1
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=4
#SBATCH --mem=16G
#SBATCH --time=02:00:00
#SBATCH --output=slurm-%j.out
#SBATCH --error=slurm-%j.err
#SBATCH --mail-type=END,FAIL
# inside the script run your commands
module load python/3.10
srun python train.py --epochs 10

Notes:
- #SBATCH lines are parsed by Slurm; place them before other non-comment lines.
- Use srun inside the script to launch the job step(s); srun will use the resources requested by SBATCH.

4) Requesting GPUs and other resources
- GPUs: #SBATCH --gres=gpu:2 (or --gres=gpu:V100:2 on some clusters)
- Memory per node or per CPU: --mem=32G or --mem-per-cpu=4G
- Select node features/constraints: --constraint=haswell or --constraint="gpu & large-mem"
- Partition (queue): --partition=gpu

5) Interactive examples
- Quick interactive shell on compute nodes:
  salloc --nodes=1 --ntasks=1 --cpus-per-task=4 --time=01:00:00 --gres=gpu:1 --pty bash
- Or run a single command on allocated resources:
  srun --ntasks=4 hostname

6) Job arrays and dependencies
- Job array Example: #SBATCH --array=0-99%10
  - Creates 100 tasks but runs at most 10 concurrently.
- Dependencies:
  - sbatch --dependency=afterok:<jobid> step2.sh
  - Useful for multi-stage pipelines.

7) Monitoring and debugging
- Show queued/running jobs: squeue -u $USER or squeue -j <jobid>
- Show reason for pending jobs: squeue -o "%.18i %.9P %.20j %.8u %.2t %.10M %.9l %.6D %R" or scontrol show job <jobid>
  - Common pending reasons: Resources, QOSLimit, Priority, ReqNodeNotAvail, Dependency.
- Check nodes/partitions: sinfo -s (summary) or sinfo -N -l (per-node)
- Per-job runtime stats: sstat -j <jobid>
- After completion, check accounting: sacct -j <jobid> --format=JobID,JobName,State,Elapsed,ExitCode

8) Useful scontrol commands (read-only vs admin)
- Read details: scontrol show job <jobid>, scontrol show node <nodename>
- (Admin-only mutating commands exist, e.g., scontrol update, drain/resume nodes — contact your admin/operator to run those.)

9) Output, working directory, and environment
- By default stdout/stderr go to files set by --output/--error; otherwise slurm-<jobid>.out in the submission directory.
- SLURM supplies environment variables inside jobs: SLURM_JOB_ID, SLURM_NTASKS, SLURM_JOB_NODELIST, SLURM_CPUS_ON_NODE, etc.
- Always load necessary modules inside the script (module load …) to get reproducible runs.

10) Troubleshooting tips
- Job pending for long: check squeue & sinfo. If reason is "Resources", cluster is busy; consider smaller resource requests or different partition/time.
- ExitCode nonzero: inspect stderr/stdout; sacct will show ExitCode and elapsed.
- If your job doesn’t start because of QOS/account limits, speak to admins or check sacctmgr/qos settings.
- For MPI jobs, use srun (not mpirun) or configure mpirun to use Slurm env vars; ensure proper binding and --ntasks/--nodes.

11) Good practices
- Request realistic resources (over-requesting wastes scheduler opportunities).
- Use time limits that match expected runtime; jobs killed for exceeding time appear as TIMEOUT.
- Use job arrays for many similar tasks (instead of many separate sbatch calls).
- Redirect logs and preserve intermediate outputs to persistent storage.
- Test interactively with small resource requests before large production runs.

12) Where to read more
- man pages: sbatch(1), srun(1), squeue(1), sinfo(1), sacct(1), scontrol(1)
- Official docs: https://slurm.schedmd.com

Would you like:
- a tailored example for GPUs (with modules and conda env),
- a short checklist for submitting your first job on your cluster, or
- live help inspecting your current queue/partitions (I can run sinfo/squeue if you want)?

results.prompt: Show me a safe sbatch script pattern
results.agent_response:
Below is a compact, safe sbatch script pattern you can copy and adapt. It shows common best-practices: explicit SBATCH resource directives, strict shell safety flags, robust temporary-directory handling and cleanup, sensible stdout/stderr naming, using srun for launched work, and optional signal handling for requeueing.

Example safe sbatch pattern (edit fields to your site and job):
#!/usr/bin/env bash
#SBATCH --job-name=myjob               # job name
#SBATCH --output=%x-%j.out             # %x = job name, %j = jobid
#SBATCH --error=%x-%j.err
#SBATCH --time=02:00:00                # walltime
#SBATCH --nodes=1
#SBATCH --ntasks=1
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=4
#SBATCH --mem=8G
#SBATCH --gres=gpu:1                   # remove if not using GPUs
#SBATCH --mail-type=END,FAIL
#SBATCH --mail-user=you@example.com
#SBATCH --chdir=/home/you/workdir      # absolute working directory

# ---- shell safety ----
set -euo pipefail
IFS=$'\n\t'
umask 0022

# ---- secure tmpdir and cleanup ----
TMPDIR=$(mktemp -d "${TMPDIR:-/tmp}/${SLURM_JOB_NAME:-job}-$SLURM_JOB_ID-XXXX")
export TMPDIR
cleanup() {
  rc=$?
  echo "[$(date +'%FT%T%z')] Cleaning up tmpdir $TMPDIR (exit=$rc)"
  rm -rf -- "$TMPDIR" || true
}
trap cleanup EXIT

# Optional: ask Slurm to requeue on TERM (depends on admin policy)
# trap 'scontrol requeue $SLURM_JOB_ID' TERM

# ---- environment ----
module purge
module load python/3.9 cuda/11.2         # load only what you need
# set environment variables explicitly rather than relying on inherited shell state
export OMP_NUM_THREADS=${OMP_NUM_THREADS:-4}

# ---- logging ----
echo "Job $SLURM_JOB_ID ($SLURM_JOB_NAME) starting on $(hostname) at $(date)"
echo "Allocated nodes: $SLURM_NODELIST"
echo "Temporary dir: $TMPDIR"

# ---- run work using srun ----
# prefer srun for MPI/parallel tasks so Slurm tracks processes and signals correctly
srun --cpu-bind=cores my_program --arg value

echo "Job $SLURM_JOB_ID finished at $(date)"

Key safety notes and reasoning
- Put all #SBATCH directives before any non-comment line; Slurm only reads directives up to the first real line of script.
- set -euo pipefail + IFS prevents subtle shell-scripting errors (exit on error, unset-vars treated as errors).
- Use mktemp to create a unique, private TMPDIR and trap cleanup on EXIT so temp files aren’t left behind.
- Use srun to launch the job workload — srun integrates with Slurm for cgroup/signals, accounting, and resource tracking.
- Name logs with %x (job name) and %j (job id) to avoid accidental clobbering when running multiple jobs.
- Explicit --chdir avoids surprises from submitting from different CWDs.
- Load only required modules and set OMP_NUM_THREADS / CPUS_PER_TASK consistently to avoid oversubscription.
- Consider mail/notifications for FAIL/END but be careful with mail volume for many short jobs.
- Optional: trap 'scontrol requeue $SLURM_JOB_ID' TERM can requeue preempted jobs (cluster policy permitting).
- Avoid backgrounding long lived processes without srun; background daemons may not be tracked or killed correctly by Slurm.
- Keep resource requests (mem, cpus, gpus, time) conservative and explicit to help the scheduler pack effectively.

If you want, I can:
- produce a minimal GPU/CPU-only variant,
- add an MPI multi-node example (srun --mpi=pmix_v3 ...),
- or validate a specific script you already have (paste it and I'll highlight safety issues). Which would you like?

results.prompt: Slurm tutorial
results.agent_response:
Good — here’s a compact, practical Slurm tutorial you can use as a quick reference. If you want examples tied to your cluster (partition names, GPU availability, accounts), tell me and I can inspect the live cluster for you.

Basics / key commands
- Submit a batch job: sbatch <script.sh>
- Run interactively / allocate resources: salloc [options] then srun ... OR srun --pty [options] bash
- Launch a single jobstep (interactive command): srun [options] cmd
- Show current queue: squeue (filter: -u <user>, -p <partition>, -j <jobid>)
- Show partitions / node states: sinfo
- Job details: scontrol show job <jobid>
- Historical/accounting: sacct (useful after jobs complete)
- Cancel a job: scancel <jobid>
- Scheduler diagnostics: sdiag, sprio, sprio --weights
- Licenses: scontrol license
- Reservations: scontrol show reservation

Simple sbatch script template
- Save as run.sh, then sbatch run.sh
Example content (replace options to match your cluster):
#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --job-name=myjob
#SBATCH --output=myjob.%j.out
#SBATCH --error=myjob.%j.err
#SBATCH --partition=gpu
#SBATCH --nodes=1
#SBATCH --ntasks=1
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=8
#SBATCH --gres=gpu:1
#SBATCH --time=02:00:00
#SBATCH --account=myacct
#SBATCH --qos=normal

module purge
module load python/3.10 cuda/12.0
srun python train.py --epochs 10

Key sbatch/srun options explained
- --partition / -p : partition (queue) to use
- --nodes / -N : number of nodes
- --ntasks / -n : number of MPI/rank tasks
- --cpus-per-task : CPU threads per task (for multithreaded tasks)
- --mem or --mem-per-cpu : memory (total or per CPU)
- --gres=gpu:1 : request GPUs (generic resources)
- --time : wallclock limit (HH:MM:SS or D-HH:MM:SS)
- --account / --qos : accounting/QoS requirements
- --output / --error : redirect stdout/stderr
- --mail-type / --mail-user : email notifications
- --exclusive : full node exclusive use

Interactive GPU session example
- srun --partition=gpu --gres=gpu:1 --cpus-per-task=8 --pty bash
or with allocation:
- salloc --partition=gpu --gres=gpu:1 --cpus-per-task=8
- srun --pty bash

Job arrays
- Submit many similar tasks: sbatch --array=1-100%10 array_job.sh
- Inside script use $SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID to pick dataset/parameter for that array index.
- %10 limits concurrent array tasks to 10.

Dependencies
- Chain jobs: sbatch --dependency=afterok:<jobid> next_job.sh
- Common dependency types: after, afterok, afternotok, afterany, singleton

Checking job status and reasons
- squeue -o "%.18i %.9P %.8j %.8u %.2t %.10M %.6D %R" (custom format including reason)
- If a job is PENDING, squeue shows a reason (BeginTime, Resources, Priority, Dependency, Assoc*, etc.). For extra detail: scontrol show job <jobid>.
- Common pending reasons: Dependency, Priority, Resources, QOSLimit, Association limit exceeded.

When jobs fail or are killed
- Use sacct -j <jobid> --format=JobID,JobName,State,ExitCode,Elapsed,MaxRSS to inspect exit codes and memory use (after job is finished).
- OUT_OF_MEMORY and ExitCode indicate memory issues — increase --mem or --mem-per-cpu or reduce memory usage.
- If a job exits with non-zero but no stderr, check the node-specific logs or the job’s .err file.

Resource-request tips
- Choose cpus-per-task for threaded apps (OpenMP/NumPy).
- Choose ntasks (and tasks-per-node) for MPI.
- Use --mem vs --mem-per-cpu depending on how memory is charged on your cluster.
- GPUs: request with --gres=gpu:<count> and use the device(s) shown via nvidia-smi; Slurm usually sets CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES for you.

Output, logs, and reproducibility
- Use --output and --error (or combined --output=...%j.out for jobid) so logs are per-job.
- Save random seeds and environment dump (module list, pip freeze) in output for reproducibility.

Advanced topics (short)
- Preemption / QOS: some partitions may preempt lower-QoS jobs.
- Check fairshare / priorities: sshare (fairshare) and sprio (per-job priority).
- Requeueing: sbatch --requeue or scontrol requeue <jobid> (admin).
- Checkpointing: use application-level checkpointing; Slurm can support epilog/prolog but isn’t an app checkpoint system.
- Reservations: scontrol show reservation <name> to inspect reserved time windows.
- Licenses: scontrol license shows license usage.

Troubleshooting checklist (pending / not starting)
1. squeue -j <jobid> → note the REASON column.
2. If reason unclear: scontrol show job <jobid> for detailed info.
3. Check partition/node availability: sinfo
4. Check account/QoS limits: sacctmgr show user or ask admins.
5. If nodes are drained/down: sinfo -R or sinfo_reasons to see node reasons.

Useful examples
- Cancel all your pending jobs: scancel -u $USER -t PENDING
- Show last 7 days of your jobs: sacct -u $USER --starttime=now-7days
- Submit job array and use task ID: sbatch --array=1-10 job.sh (use $SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID)

Where to learn more / next steps
- Read Slurm manpages: sbatch(1), srun(1), squeue(1), sinfo(1), sacct(1)
- Cluster-specific docs: your cluster’s user guide (partition names, accounts, module environment, GPU model)
- If you want, I can:
  - Show your cluster’s partitions/nodes (sinfo)
  - Inspect a specific job ID (squeue + scontrol show job)
  - Help convert a local script to an sbatch script
  - Draft an sbatch script tuned for GPU training

Which of those would you like next? (If you want me to inspect your cluster state or a job, tell me the job ID or partition name and I’ll run the appropriate Slurm read commands.)

results.prompt: Slurm tutorial
results.agent_response:
Good — here’s a concise Slurm tutorial covering the core concepts, common commands, example job scripts, and troubleshooting tips so you can get started quickly.

1) Core concepts
- Slurm components: slurmctld (controller), slurmd (daemon on each compute node), optional slurmdbd (accounting), and slurmrestd (REST API).
- Jobs: submitted work units (batch or interactive). Job steps are sub-tasks within a job.
- Partitions: logical groupings of nodes (like queues).
- Resources: CPUs, memory, GPUs, licenses, nodes. Request them when submitting.
- States: PENDING, RUNNING, COMPLETED, FAILED, CANCELLED, TIMEOUT, etc.

2) Most-used commands (quick)
- sbatch script.sh — submit a batch job (non-interactive).
- srun [options] command — run a task (can be used inside a job or for interactive runs).
- salloc [options] — allocate an interactive job (gives you a shell on compute nodes).
- squeue — view queued/running jobs.
- sinfo — view partition/node availability and states.
- scancel <jobid> — cancel a job.
- scontrol show job <jobid> — detailed job info (reasons, TRES, etc).
- sacct — accounting: view historical/completed job records.
- sstat -j <jobid> — runtime stats for a running job (CPU/memory I/O).
- sreport — resource usage reports.
- scontrol show config / scontrol ping — controller configs/health.

3) Example sbatch script (basic)
#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --job-name=myjob
#SBATCH --output=slurm-%j.out
#SBATCH --error=slurm-%j.err
#SBATCH --time=02:00:00            # HH:MM:SS
#SBATCH --nodes=1
#SBATCH --ntasks=1
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=4
#SBATCH --mem=16G
#SBATCH --partition=standard
#SBATCH --gres=gpu:1               # request 1 GPU (if available)

module load python/3.10
srun python train.py --epochs 10

Notes:
- Use --output / --error to capture stdout/stderr (default is slurm-%j.out).
- --gres=gpu:N requests GPUs. If GPUs are managed, Slurm or the plugin will set CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES appropriately.
- Replace module load / container commands as your site requires.

4) Interactive usage examples
- Quick interactive allocation: salloc --time=01:00:00 --ntasks=1 --cpus-per-task=4 --mem=8G
  then run srun --pty bash to get a shell on an allocated node.
- Direct single-command interactive (no allocation shell): srun --pty --time=00:30:00 /bin/bash

5) Job arrays and dependencies
- Arrays: sbatch --array=1-100%10 job-array.sh
  Use $SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID inside the script to index work. %10 limits concurrent array tasks.
- Dependencies: sbatch --dependency=afterok:<jobid> job.sh (or afterany, afterok:job1:job2, etc.)

6) Typical resource-request flags
- --nodes=<N>, --ntasks=<tasks>, --cpus-per-task=<threads>, --mem=<per-node|per-cpu> (e.g., 4G or 16G)
- --time=HH:MM:SS
- --partition=<name>, --qos=<qos-name>, --account=<acct>
- --gres=gpu:<count> or --gres=gpu:V100:2 for type-specific (if supported)
- --constraint=<label> to pick nodes with specific features

7) Useful environment variables inside jobs
- SLURM_JOB_ID, SLURM_JOB_NODELIST (nodes assigned), SLURM_NTASKS, SLURM_CPUS_PER_TASK, SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID, etc.

8) Checking job status and debugging
- squeue -u $USER or squeue -j <jobid> shows current state and (usually) PENDING reason column.
- If squeue doesn’t show a reason for a pending job, scontrol show job <jobid> shows detailed pending reason.
- Look at job stdout/stderr files (slurm-<jobid>.out or files you set with --output/--error).
- For running jobs, sstat -j <jobid> can show live memory/CPU usage.
- sacct --format=JobID,JobName,State,ExitCode,Elapsed -j <jobid> for post-mortem accounting.

Common pending reasons: Resources (no matching resources free), Priority (lower priority), QOS or Account limits, Dependency (waiting on other jobs), Partition down/drain, Reservation required.

9) Best practices
- Test with a small resource/time request first.
- Always set a realistic time limit; short limits help scheduler backfill.
- Capture stdout/stderr to files and include job name in outputs for debugging.
- Use job arrays for many similar short tasks to reduce scheduler overhead.
- Use modules or containers to reproduce environments; prefer read-only data paths and write outputs to $SCRATCH.
- For long-running work, implement checkpointing so you can restart from the last good state.

10) Accounting and reporting
- sacct shows historical job outcomes and resource usage (CPU-hours, walltime).
- sreport can produce usage summaries by user/account/partition for billing or reporting.

11) Advanced: GPUs, multi-node MPI, containers
- GPUs: request with --gres=gpu:N. Within a job, verify CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES or use nvidia-smi on the node to see assigned GPUs.
- MPI: typically launched with srun -n <ranks> or mpirun inside an allocation depending on your MPI and cluster config.
- Containers: run singularity/apptainer or Docker (via helpers) inside the job script; srun can wrap container exec commands.

12) Quick reference examples
- Submit: sbatch job.sh
- See your queue: squeue -u $(whoami)
- See partitions: sinfo -s
- Cancel: scancel <jobid>
- Inspect: scontrol show job <jobid>
- Account history: sacct -u alice --starttime=2024-01-01

If you want
- a short interactive walkthrough (I can run sinfo/squeue/sacct for your cluster) — tell me which and I’ll run the appropriate read-only commands, or
- a runnable example tailored to your cluster (GPU vs CPU, node sizes) — tell me target resources and I’ll produce a ready-to-submit script.

Which would you like next: a sample job tuned to GPUs/CPU, or a live inspection of queue/partitions on your cluster?

results.prompt: Show me a safe sbatch script pattern
results.agent_response:
Below is a concise, safe sbatch script pattern you can copy and adapt. It focuses on predictable failure handling, reliable logging, proper use of Slurm environment variables, and clean temporary-directory handling.

#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --job-name=example_job         # short name
#SBATCH --output=%x-%j.out            # %x=job-name %j=jobid
#SBATCH --error=%x-%j.err
#SBATCH --time=01:00:00               # HH:MM:SS
#SBATCH --partition=gpu               # partition (edit)
#SBATCH --gres=gpu:1                  # request GPU(s) if needed
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=4
#SBATCH --mem=16G
#SBATCH --mail-type=END,FAIL          # optional notifications
#SBATCH --mail-user=you@example.com

# Fail early and portably, avoid word-splitting surprises
set -euo pipefail
IFS=$'\n\t'

# ---------- cleanup & signal handling ----------
cleanup() {
  rc=$?
  echo "$(date -Is) CLEANUP: exit status $rc"
  # Example cleanup actions:
  # rm -rf "$TMPDIR"
  # kill background children if any
  exit $rc
}
trap cleanup EXIT INT TERM

# ---------- basic environment sanity ----------
echo "Starting job $SLURM_JOB_ID ($SLURM_JOB_NAME) on $(hostname)"
echo "Nodes: ${SLURM_JOB_NODELIST:-N/A}  CPUs/task: ${SLURM_CPUS_PER_TASK:-N/A}"

# always run in the directory where sbatch was invoked
cd "${SLURM_SUBMIT_DIR:-$PWD}"

# set reasonable defaults that depend on sbatch settings
export OMP_NUM_THREADS=${SLURM_CPUS_PER_TASK:-1}

# per-job temporary directory (cleanup in cleanup())
TMPDIR="${TMPDIR:-/tmp/$USER/.$SLURM_JOB_ID}"
mkdir -p "$TMPDIR"
export TMPDIR

# ---------- load environment / modules ----------
module purge
module load python/3.9  # adapt to your site
# source venv if you use one
# source ./venv/bin/activate

# ---------- run work ----------
# Use srun for parallel/mpi tasks so Slurm launches steps correctly
srun --mpi=pmix_v3 python train.py --epochs 10 --data /path/to/data

# For single-process jobs you may call the command directly:
# python step.sh

# ---------- optional: explicit exit ----------
echo "Job $SLURM_JOB_ID completed"
exit 0

Notes and best practices
- set -euo pipefail + IFS prevents silent failures and word-splitting bugs. The trap+cleanup ensures temporary files are removed and the original exit code is preserved.
- Use SLURM env vars (SLURM_JOB_ID, SLURM_SUBMIT_DIR, SLURM_CPUS_PER_TASK, SLURM_JOB_NODELIST, SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID) rather than guessing node names or IDs.
- Prefer srun to launch task steps (MPI, multi-node) so Slurm can manage resource binding and environment (and set CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES for GPUs).
- Keep outputs predictable: use --output/--error patterns with %x/%j or explicit paths. Don’t rely on the remote shell to capture logs.
- Create per-job TMPDIR under local /tmp or a fast scratch, and remove it in cleanup. Avoid race conditions by using $SLURM_JOB_ID in names.
- Don’t assume environment modules or PATH items are present — load what you need inside the script.
- Be careful with secret credentials: avoid hard-coding; read from a secure location only when necessary and ensure they’re removed after use.
- Test script syntax locally with bash -n script.sh and dry-run small jobs before large-scale runs.

If you want, I can produce:
- a minimal one-liner version,
- an array-job friendly template showing SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID usage,
- or a GPU/torch-specific template (CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES notes). Which would you like?

results.prompt: Explain basic Slurm submission steps
results.agent_response:
Below is a concise, practical checklist of the basic steps and concepts for submitting jobs to Slurm (sbatch), plus a minimal example and a few troubleshooting tips.

1) Create a batch script
- Start with a shell shebang (#!/bin/bash or /bin/sh).
- Add SBATCH header directives (one per line) before any non-comment/non-whitespace line:
  - Common directives: --partition (or -p), --account (-A), --time, --nodes, --ntasks, --cpus-per-task, --mem, --gres (e.g., gres=gpu:1), --qos, --job-name, --output, --error, --mail-type/--mail-user.
- Put the commands to run after the SBATCH lines (module loads, environment setup, srun/mpirun, your program).

2) Minimal example
#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --job-name=myjob
#SBATCH --partition=gpu
#SBATCH --nodes=1
#SBATCH --ntasks=1
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=4
#SBATCH --gres=gpu:1
#SBATCH --time=02:00:00
#SBATCH --output=slurm-%j.out

module load cuda
srun ./my_program arg1 arg2

3) Submit the job
- sbatch myscript.sh
- sbatch prints a job ID (e.g., “Submitted batch job 12345”) and exits immediately. The job may remain PENDING until resources are available.

4) Check job and cluster status
- squeue to see queued/running jobs (use -u $USER to filter).
- sinfo to view partition/node availability and states.
- sacct for historical/completed job accounting (after or for older jobs).

5) Running steps vs batch script commands
- Use srun inside the batch script to launch tasks under the Slurm allocation (recommended for MPI and parallel jobs).
- Don’t use srun to submit the script itself — sbatch is for batch submission. Use salloc/srun for interactive allocations.

6) Job arrays and dependencies
- Arrays: sbatch --array=1-100%10 myscript.sh (use % to limit concurrent array tasks).
- Dependencies: sbatch --dependency=afterok:12345 to hold until another job finishes successfully.

7) Environment and useful variables
- Slurm sets variables inside the job: SLURM_JOB_ID, SLURM_NTASKS, SLURM_NODELIST, etc.
- Default stdout/stderr go to a file like slurm-%j.out unless you set --output/--error.

8) Output, logs, and debugging
- Redirect or set --output/--error for logs.
- If job is pending, squeue may show a Reason; scontrol show job JOBID gives detailed info.
- For runtime debugging, run a small test with short time/one node, or use srun interactively.

9) Cancelling and modifying
- Cancel: scancel JOBID
- Change time limit or other attributes requires operator tools (scontrol update) — contact admins where required.

10) Common tips
- Request only the resources you need (over-requesting increases queue time).
- Use modules or virtualenvs inside the script so the job environment is reproducible.
- For GPU jobs, request GPUs with --gres=gpu:N and ensure you pick the proper partition.
- Use --mem vs --mem-per-cpu carefully depending on how memory is accounted.

If you want, I can:
- Review a job script you have and point out improvements; or
- Show a short example for MPI, GPU deep learning, or a job-array script. Which would you like?

results.prompt: How do I submit a job?
results.agent_response:
Short answer: write a batch script with SBATCH directives and run sbatch <script>. Below are the key points and examples.

1) Minimal batch script (myjob.sh)
- Top line and SBATCH directives set resources and metadata.
- Commands after directives run on the allocated nodes.

Example:
#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --job-name=myjob
#SBATCH --output=%x.%j.out
#SBATCH --error=%x.%j.err
#SBATCH --ntasks=1
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=4
#SBATCH --mem=16G
#SBATCH --time=02:00:00
#SBATCH --partition=gpu
#SBATCH --gres=gpu:2
#SBATCH --account=projectname
#SBATCH --mail-type=END,FAIL
#SBATCH --mail-user=you@domain.tld

module load python
srun python train.py   # or the command(s) you need

Submit:
- sbatch myjob.sh
  - sbatch prints the job ID (e.g., "Submitted batch job 12345").

2) Useful sbatch command-line shortcuts
- Inline/simple: sbatch --job-name=quick --time=00:10:00 --wrap="python quick.py"
- Dependency: --dependency=afterok:<jobid>
- Array jobs: add #SBATCH --array=1-10 and use $SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID in the script

3) Interactive / short-run alternatives
- salloc / srun --pty bash for an interactive allocation (useful for debugging or interactive runs).
- srun inside a batch script runs your parallel tasks under the allocation.

4) Common checks and controls
- Check queue: squeue -u $USER or squeue -j <jobid>
- Detailed job info: scontrol show job <jobid>
- Cancel: scancel <jobid>

5) Tips
- Always request realistic time and memory to avoid early kill or scheduler penalties.
- Use output and error files to capture logs (%j substitutes jobid, %x jobname).
- For GPUs use --gres=gpu:N and confirm partition supports GPUs (ask if unsure).
- If you need account/QOS, add --account=... or --qos=...

If you want, tell me: what command/script do you want to run and what resources (CPUs, memory, GPUs, walltime, partition, account)? I can draft a ready-to-submit myjob.sh for you.

results.prompt: Explain queue priority using fairshare, Fair Tree usage, and configured priority weights
results.agent_response:
Short answer first: Slurm schedules by computing a single job priority number from several independent "factors" and their configured integer weights. Fair-share (the fairshare factor) is one of those factors; when Slurm is configured to use the Fair Tree algorithm, fairshare is computed by ranking associations in a tree so that account/association hierarchy is respected. The final job priority is the weighted sum of enabled factors (age, fairshare, job size, QOS, partition, TRES usage, site, etc.), and the configured PriorityWeight* values in slurm.conf determine each factor's influence.

Details

1) The multifactor priority model (what actually runs)
- When PriorityType=priority/multifactor the scheduler computes:
  Job_priority = site_factor
                 + PriorityWeightAge * age_factor
                 + PriorityWeightAssoc * assoc_factor
                 + PriorityWeightFairshare * fairshare_factor
                 + PriorityWeightJobSize * job_size_factor
                 + PriorityWeightPartition * partition_factor
                 + PriorityWeightQOS * QOS_factor
                 + (sum of TRES_weight_X * TRES_factor_X)
                 - nice_factor
- Each "factor" is a floating value in [0.0, 1.0] (unless maxed), while PriorityWeight* are unsigned integers. The sum is scaled into Slurm's integer priority range (0..4294967295). Higher numeric priority = scheduled earlier.

2) Fairshare vs. Fair Tree
- Fairshare purpose: favor queued jobs for users/accounts that have been under-served historically, and deprioritize those that have consumed more than their share.
- Classic fairshare (older algorithm) computed factors per-account/user in a simple usage-vs-shares way.
- Fair Tree (default since Slurm 19.05) computes a level-based fairshare by walking the account/user association tree:
  - It computes a Level Fairshare among siblings, sorts children by that value, and does a depth-first (pre-order) traversal to produce a global ranking of associations.
  - Each association’s fairshare_factor is its rank / total_associations (highest-ranked = 1.0).
- Key Fair Tree properties:
  - Honors account hierarchy: if account A outranks sibling B, all children of A outrank all children of B.
  - Produces stable, well-ordered rankings (avoids numerical precision ties).
  - Requires SlurmDBD/accounting so usage and share values are known.
- Operational consequence: Fair Tree creates a global ordered ranking, not just a local usage ratio. That means small changes in weights can have large effects unless weights are tuned.

3) Configured priority weights and related parameters
- Common weights in slurm.conf:
  - PriorityWeightFairshare — multiplies the fairshare factor.
  - PriorityWeightAge — multiplies how long a job has been eligible to run (age_factor).
  - PriorityWeightAssoc — association/account weighting.
  - PriorityWeightJobSize — favors small or large jobs depending on configuration.
  - PriorityWeightPartition, PriorityWeightQOS — give priority boost for partition or QOS.
  - TRES weights (TRESWeightX / TRESWeightCpu etc.) — weight by requested resource amounts.
- Decay / timing parameters:
  - PriorityDecayHalfLife (aka PriorityDecayHalfLife / PriorityCalcPeriod) — controls how quickly historical usage decays for fairshare calculations. Longer half-life → older usage matters longer.
  - PriorityCalcPeriod — how often the priority plugin recalculates.
  - PriorityUsageResetPeriod — optional reset of usage counters if you want hard periodic resets.
  - PriorityMaxAge — how long age_factor grows before it stops (caps at 1.0), used to limit starvation.
- Practical tuning notes:
  - Weights are relative: raising one weight increases that factor’s influence versus the others.
  - If you use Fair Tree, administrators often set PriorityWeightFairshare smaller than older “classic” setups because Fair Tree's ranking can dominate; e.g., a much smaller fairshare weight (1–10) may suffice compared to older setups.
  - Age_factor is the usual counterbalance to prevent starvation: if fairshare keeps deprioritizing a user, age will eventually lift that user’s jobs.
  - TRES weights let you prefer e.g., small-CPU jobs or GPU jobs by adding positive weight for the desired resources.
  - QOS/partition weights let you implement administrative priorities (service queues, production users).

4) Interactions and examples
- Example 1: If PriorityWeightFairshare is very large and Fair Tree is used, under-served accounts' jobs will almost always run before others—even if their jobs are large—until their usage catches up.
- Example 2: If PriorityWeightAge is large, long-waiting jobs will climb rapidly regardless of fairshare, preventing starvation but reducing short-term fairness.
- Example 3: Use moderate PriorityWeightFairshare + moderate PriorityWeightAge to balance fairness and job latency.
- Example 4: To favor small jobs, increase PriorityWeightJobSize so the job_size_factor gives small jobs a higher factor.

5) How to inspect & debug (commands to run as admin/user)
- sshare -l : show fairshare values and Level FS for associations (useful to understand Fair Tree outputs).
- sprio -l : show per-job factor contributions and the final priority breakdown for queued jobs.
- scontrol show config | grep -i Priority : view current PriorityWeight* and Priority* timing parameters.
- sdiag / sprio_weights : extra scheduler diagnostics and current weight settings.
- sprio_weights (or sprio --weights) shows the configured weight contributions that sprio uses.

6) Practical recommendations
- Start simple: pick 2–3 dominant factors (fairshare, age, job size or TRES) and tune them incrementally.
- If you move from Classic fairshare to Fair Tree, reduce PriorityWeightFairshare and monitor sprio/sshare to see real effects.
- Use PriorityDecayHalfLife to control how quickly past usage becomes irrelevant; short half-life enforces recent fairness, long half-life enforces long-term fairness.
- Monitor sprio and sshare regularly after changes to ensure you didn’t accidentally starve a user group.
- When in doubt, test in a staging environment or with controlled job submissions to observe scheduler behavior before changing production weights.

If you want, I can:
- Show the current configured PriorityWeight* values on your cluster (scontrol show config) and the current fairshare values (sshare -l) so we can discuss concrete tuning—would you like me to fetch those?

results.prompt: Explain queue priority using fairshare, Fair Tree usage, and configured priority weights
results.agent_response:
Short answer first
- Slurm uses the multifactor priority plugin (PriorityType=priority/multifactor) to compute a single integer job priority as a weighted sum of several normalized factors (age, fair‑share, job size, QOS, partition, TRES, site factor, etc.).
- Fairshare is the factor that rewards under‑served accounts/users and de‑prioritizes over‑served ones; Fair Tree is Slurm’s modern algorithm for computing the fairshare factor from accounting data.
- Priority weights (the PriorityWeight* and TRES_weight_* settings in slurm.conf) scale each normalized factor before they are summed; tuning these weights controls how strongly each factor influences scheduling order.

How priority is calculated (high level)
- A job’s priority ≈ site_factor + PriorityWeightAge * age_factor + PriorityWeightAssoc * assoc_factor + PriorityWeightFairshare * fairshare_factor + PriorityWeightJobSize * job_size_factor + PriorityWeightPartition * partition_factor + PriorityWeightQOS * qos_factor + SUM(TRES_weight_X * TRES_factor_X) - nice_factor
- Each factor (age_factor, fairshare_factor, etc.) is normalized to a floating value typically in [0.0, 1.0]. Weights are integer multipliers (0 .. 2^32-1). The final priority is an integer; larger = higher priority.

Fairshare (concept)
- Purpose: steer scheduling so users/accounts who have received less of the cluster’s resources in the measured interval get higher priority for future runs. It’s not a hard quota—just a prioritization mechanism.
- Requires Slurm accounting (slurmdbd + accounting DB) because it needs historical usage and configured shares.

Fair Tree (how it works and implications)
- Fair Tree is the default fairshare algorithm (since ~19.05). It ranks all associations (accounts/users) by recursively computing level fairshare values on the account/user tree and visiting nodes in a deterministic depth‑first order.
- The user’s fairshare_factor returned by Fair Tree is a relative rank scaled to [0..1] (highest ranked user gets 1.0; others are rank/total_associations).
- Key properties:
  - Hierarchy-aware: if account A outranks sibling B, then all children of A outrank all children of B (preserves account hierarchy).
  - Stable and precision-safe compared with the old “classic” algorithm.
  - Since it ranks all associations (active or not), it can produce large relative differences—so administrators often reduce the effective weight applied to the fairshare factor.
- Operational notes:
  - Fair Tree needs the accounting DB and runs at PriorityCalcPeriod intervals. scontrol reconfigure may not force an immediate rerun.
  - You can inspect outcome with sshare -l.

Configured priority weights (what they do and tuning)
- Names: PriorityWeightAge, PriorityWeightFairshare, PriorityWeightJobSize, PriorityWeightPartition, PriorityWeightQOS, PriorityWeightAssoc, etc., plus TRES_weight_* entries for resource‑specific weighting (e.g., TRES_weight_gpu).
- Effect: the weight multiplies its factor. A higher weight makes that factor dominate the final priority ordering.
- Defaults and examples:
  - Default numeric defaults vary by site. Examples in Slurm docs show site examples like PriorityWeightAge=1000 and PriorityWeightFairshare=10000; other doc text warns default per‑factor is 1 if not explicitly set.
  - With Fair Tree, administrators commonly make PriorityWeightFairshare small (sometimes as small as 1–2 times the number of user associations) because Fair Tree already produces a strong ordinal ranking. If PriorityWeightFairshare is too large, it will dominate age, QoS, and other factors.
- TRES weights: use these to bias priorities by resource consumption — e.g., give jobs requesting GPUs higher or lower priority relative to CPU‑only jobs.
- Age factor: controlled by PriorityMaxAge — age_factor ramps to 1.0 after that configured wait time. Use PriorityWeightAge to decide how strongly waiting time should overcome other penalties.
- Decay and historical window:
  - PriorityDecayHalfLife determines how fast past usage decays when computing fairshare. Larger half‑life = past usage affects priority longer.
  - PriorityUsageResetPeriod can periodically reset usage counters; useful if you want a clean slate on a cadence.
  - PriorityCalcPeriod controls how often fairshare and decay are recalculated.

Practical inspection and diagnostics (commands)
- sshare -l : show current fairshare values and Level FS for associations (useful to see how Fair Tree ranked things).
- sprio -l or sprio --weights : show each queued job’s priority components and the configured weights.
- scontrol show config : view PriorityType, PriorityWeight* settings, PriorityDecayHalfLife, PriorityMaxAge, PriorityCalcPeriod.
- scontrol reconfigure : after changing weights in slurm.conf, use this to apply config (note: Fair Tree calculations happen on the next PriorityCalcPeriod run).

Tuning guidance and common pitfalls
- Don’t let PriorityWeightFairshare be overwhelmingly large if you want age/QOS/etc. to matter; with Fair Tree you often need much smaller fairshare weight than with the old classic algorithm.
- If many accounts/users are present but most are inactive, Fair Tree still ranks all—consider how that affects the numeric fairshare values and scale weights accordingly.
- Use sprio -l to see per-job factor contributions before changing weights.
- If you want “waiting time eventually wins,” set a nontrivial PriorityWeightAge and an appropriate PriorityMaxAge so long‑waiting jobs rise in priority.
- If you change from classic fairshare to Fair Tree, monitor with sshare and sprio and adjust PriorityWeightFairshare downward if fairshare becomes too dominant.
- Use PriorityDecayHalfLife to control the time horizon for “fairness.” Short half‑life (days) gives fast catch‑up for under‑served accounts; long half‑life enforces long‑term share balance.

Example scenarios (illustrative)
- Scenario A (favor fairness strongly): PriorityWeightFairshare >> PriorityWeightAge, PriorityWeightQOS. Result: under‑served accounts’ jobs jump ahead even if new.
- Scenario B (age matters): PriorityWeightAge comparable to PriorityWeightFairshare, PriorityMaxAge set so age reaches 1.0 after, e.g., 7 days. Result: jobs waiting long will eventually overtake small fairshare differences.
- Scenario C (Fair Tree + small fairshare weight): PriorityWeightFairshare set to small integer (e.g., 1–10), PriorityWeightAge = 1000, makes waiting and QOS the stronger controls while still nudging fairness.

If you want, I can:
- Show the current priority weights and fairshare values on your cluster (scontrol show config, sprio --weights, and sshare -l).  
- Or recommend a concrete weight set given your goals (e.g., favor fairness vs. favor throughput), if you tell me what you want to prioritize (fairness, throughput, turnaround time, or priority for specific groups).

Which would you like next?

## Job Priority Factors In General [#general](https://slurm.schedmd.com/priority_multifactor.html)
The job's priority at any given time will be a weighted sum of all the
factors that have been enabled in the slurm.conf file. Job priority can be
expressed as:
```text
Job_priority = site_factor + (PriorityWeightAge) * (age_factor) + (PriorityWeightAssoc) * (assoc_factor) + (PriorityWeightFairshare) * (fair-share_factor) + (PriorityWeightJobSize) * (job_size_factor) + (PriorityWeightPartition) * (priority_job_factor) + (PriorityWeightQOS) * (QOS_factor) + SUM(TRES_weight_cpu * TRES_factor_cpu, TRES_weight_ * TRES_factor_ , ...) - nice_factor
```
All of the factors in this formula are floating point numbers that
range from 0.0 to 1.0. The weights are unsigned, 32 bit integers.

## The sprio utility [#sprio](https://slurm.schedmd.com/priority_multifactor.html)
The sprio command provides a summary of the six factors
that comprise each job's scheduling priority. While squeue has
format options (%p and %Q) that display a job's composite priority,
sprio can be used to display a breakdown of the priority components
for each job. In addition, the sprio -w option displays the
weights (PriorityWeightAge, PriorityWeightFairshare, etc.) for each

sbatch submits a batch script to Slurm. The batch script may be given to

# "Configless" Slurm
"Configless" Slurm is a feature that allows the compute nodes —
specifically the slurmd process — and user commands running on login
nodes to pull configuration information directly from the slurmctld instead of
from a pre-distributed local file. Your cluster does require a central set of

results.prompt: Explain node features and how they affect placement
results.agent_response:
Quick overview — what “node features” are
- Node features are descriptive labels attached to compute nodes (e.g., gpu_v100, nvlink, infini, ssd, macos, highmem). They let users and the scheduler identify and select nodes with particular hardware, software, or site-specific attributes beyond raw CPUs/memory/GPU counts.
- Features are set in slurm.conf (NodeName lines) or via node helper plugins (NodeFeaturesPlugins/helpers.conf). Slurm also tracks ActiveFeatures and AvailableFeatures per node.

How features are used for placement
- Jobs request features with the constraint/features mechanism (sbatch/srun --constraint=<expr> or REST API features). The constraint expression is a logical filter applied to nodes. Only nodes that satisfy the expression are eligible for allocation.
  - Example simple forms: --constraint="gpu_v100" or --constraint="gpu_v100|gpu_v40" (either), or --constraint="gpu_v100&fastnet" (both required).
  - Parentheses and boolean combinations are supported so you can build more complex requirements.
- Feature matching is a hard filter: if no eligible node has the requested feature(s), the job cannot start (it will queue and wait until eligible nodes become free or are brought online).
- Because features reduce the pool of candidate nodes, overuse/overly-specific features increases queue wait time and reduces backfill opportunities.

ActiveFeatures vs AvailableFeatures and dynamic features
- ActiveFeatures = features that are currently active on a node (what the scheduler will match against).
- AvailableFeatures = features the node can provide but which are not currently active (used by cloud/power-save helpers).
- If NodeFeaturesPlugins/helpers are configured (cloud or "rebootable" features), a job that requests an Available but not Active feature may cause the controller to allocate that node and activate the feature (for cloud nodes this can trigger a power-on or helper action). That can add latency (boot/reconfigure) before the job starts.
- Features not managed by NodeFeaturesPlugins are always considered active.

Practical implications and gotchas
- Requesting a feature can implicitly cause nodes to be powered on or rebooted if helpers/plugins are in use. That can make start time longer even if node counts look "idle".
- A feature is not a resource accounting object (unlike GRES). If you need exclusive tracking or scheduling of physical devices (GPUs, licenses), prefer GRES for device accounting and use features to describe node-level traits (e.g., GPU model).
- Mixing many orthogonal features (e.g., gpu_v100, nvlink, ssd, highmem) can fragment capacity; design feature naming so jobs can request only what they truly need.
- Admins can change ActiveFeatures with scontrol (scontrol update NodeName=... ActiveFeatures=...), but some feature changes may require a reboot (RebootProgram) if made via helpers.

How Slurm evaluates placement at allocation time
1. Scheduler filters candidates by partition, QoS, available resources (CPUs/Memory/GRES), and then by node features/constraint expression.
2. Only nodes whose ActiveFeatures satisfy the constraint expression remain eligible.
3. If NodeFeaturesPlugins mark features as available but inactive, the scheduler may choose such a node and then trigger the helper to activate the feature (cloud/power-save behavior).
4. From the remaining eligible nodes, Slurm applies its normal placement/packing policies (SelectType, SelectTypeParameters, and scheduler backfill/best-fit behavior).

Commands to inspect and manage features
- Inspect a node’s features (active/available): scontrol show node=<node>
- See features in sinfo output (per-node or partition-level): sinfo -N -o "%N %f %t"
- Change active features (admin): scontrol update NodeName=<node> ActiveFeatures=<list>
- View helpers/feature plugin behavior: check helpers.conf and slurm.conf NodeFeaturesPlugins settings (admin)

Best practices
- Use GRES for devices you need accounting/consumption for (GPUs, licenses); use features for node characteristics.
- Keep feature naming consistent and documented (prefixes for device types, network, storage, etc.).
- Avoid overly specific features unless you actually need to pin jobs to particular hardware.
- If you use dynamic features (helpers/cloud), document the startup latency so users understand potential delays.
- Offer partition-level aliases for common selections (e.g., a gpu_v100 partition) to simplify user constraints and improve scheduler efficiency.

If you want, I can:
- Show the current features and Active/AvailableFeatures for nodes on your cluster (I can run scontrol/sinfo to list them), or
- Help craft recommended feature names and constraint examples for your workloads. Which would you like?

results.prompt: Explain sinfo node states such as idle, alloc, drain, and down
results.agent_response:
Good question — sinfo reports compact node state codes that tell you whether a node can accept work and (if not) why. Below are the common states you’ll see and what they mean in practice.

- IDLE
  - The node has no running jobs and is available to accept new jobs. Shown as "idle" in sinfo.
  - Users can be scheduled onto these nodes immediately (subject to partition/QOS/constraints).

- ALLOC (ALLOCATED)
  - The node has been allocated to one or more jobs. It is not available for new allocations.
  - You may also see ALLOCATED+ (or an appended +) when the node has active jobs and additional jobs are in the process of starting/being placed.

- MIXED
  - Part of the node’s resources (CPUs/GPUs) are in use while other parts are free. Happens when multiple jobs share a node.
  - sinfo may show a node as MIXED rather than purely ALLOC or IDLE.

- DRAIN / DRAINING / DRAINED
  - DRAINING: The node has been marked to stop taking new jobs; existing jobs are allowed to finish. Shown while drain is in progress.
  - DRAIN / DRAINED: After draining completes (no running jobs remain) the node is in a drained state and will not be scheduled until explicitly returned to service.
  - Admins put nodes into drain for maintenance, upgrades, or to take them out of rotation.

- DOWN
  - The node is not responding or has been declared unavailable. It will not be allocated to jobs.
  - A non-responsive node may be moved into DOWN automatically (or by admin) and usually needs investigation or repair.

- FAIL / FAILING
  - The node experienced a failure (hardware/OS) or is in the process of being marked as failed. It will not be allocated.

- COMPLETING
  - Jobs are finishing on the node (it’s in the process of being freed). Often seen briefly as jobs complete.

- RESERV (reserved) / MAINT (maintenance)
  - The node is reserved for a reservation or maintenance window and will not be allocated for normal jobs during that reservation.

Suffix flags (single-character markers) you may encounter in sinfo:
  - ~ : node not responding (will not be allocated)
  - * or + : special allocation flags (e.g., allocated plus pending)
  - ! , % : pending or in-progress powerdown/powerup
  - $ : node in a reservation flagged for maintenance
  - @ , ^ : reboot pending/issued
  - - : node is planned by the backfill scheduler for a higher-priority job

How to get more detail
  - sinfo -N -l  (node-oriented long listing) shows per-node state and resources.
  - sinfo -R  (or sinfo_reasons) lists nodes in DOWN/DRAIN states with reasons.
  - scontrol show node=<nodename> provides full key=value details (reason, features, state flags).

Typical lifecycle example
  - idle → alloc (job starts) → completing (job finishing) → idle (if returned)  
  - admin drains node: alloc → draining → drained → admin brings it back → idle  
  - nonresponsive: becomes down (needs admin intervention)

If you want, tell me a node name or paste your sinfo output and I can explain the exact states and any reason text shown.
